United Kingdom 1946–Present
The years after 1945 opened a new chapter for the United Kingdom. Victory had exhausted the economy and transformed the state’s role; the general election of 1945 and the Labour governments that followed built the welfare state, nationalised core industries, and managed imperial retreat while the Cold War remade Britain’s alliances. The sterling crises, the end of the Raj, the founding of NATO, and the long debate over Europe all sat inside a single generation’s experience of recovery and relative decline.
From the 1950s through the 1970s the country moved through consensus politics and its undoing: full employment and stop-go economics, Suez and decolonisation, immigration and race relations, industrial conflict, Northern Ireland, and the struggle over inflation and union power. The 1979 election and the governments that followed reordered industrial relations, privatisation, and the terms of economic policy, while Europe, the Commonwealth, and the special relationship with the United States remained the fixed points of external strategy.
The later twentieth and early twenty-first centuries brought further redefinition of the Union itself—devolution to Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland—alongside globalisation, financialisation, and renewed constitutional argument. This knowledge base gathers primary and secondary witnesses for the whole post-war span: annuals, memoirs, official histories, and monographs that fix political, economic, social, and imperial themes as their authors recorded them.

Scholarly surveys / narrative histories

Britain Since 1945 (Hollowell, ed., Blackwell 2003) — Making Contemporary Britain multi-author survey: twenty-three chapters on post-war politics (foreign policy, constitution, parties, Commonwealth→Europe, Scotland, Wales, NI, civil service, media), society (class, women, culture, education, race, health, science, pressure groups), and economy (policy, employment, industrial relations, welfare state).
The People’s Peace: Britain Since 1945 (Morgan, 4th ed. OUP 2021) — Single-author political narrative from Attlee and the post-war settlement through consensus and retreat, Thatcherism, New Labour, crash, and Brexit (1945–2020).

Investigative monographs / contemporary polemics

Dope, Inc.: Britain’s Opium War Against the United States (Kalimtgis, Goldman, Steinberg, 1978) — U.S. Labor Party report presenting the world narcotics trade as a British-centered political-warfare and banking system from the Opium Wars through Hong Kong, Canada, organized crime, and the 1960s counterculture.
Dope, Inc.: Britain’s Opium War against the World (Editors of EIR, 4th ed., 2010) — Updated EIR compilation: LaRouche war plan, Afghan opium, Soros/decrim, multi-hundred-billion trade estimates, and reprinted Opium War / organized-crime cores from earlier editions.
A Century of War: Anglo-American Oil Politics and the New World Order (Engdahl, rev. English ed. 2011; first English 1992) — Oil geopolitics from late British Empire free trade and the three imperial pillars through two world wars, petrodollars, and early twenty-first-century energy wars.
Devil’s Game: How the United States Helped Unleash Fundamentalist Islam (Dreyfuss, 2005) — American Empire Project history of U.S. (and earlier British) cultivation of political Islam from pan-Islam and the Muslim Brotherhood through the Afghan jihad and the clash-of-civilizations debate.
Secret Affairs: Britain’s Collusion with Radical Islam (Curtis, updated ed. 2018; first 2010) — Documented Whitehall collusion with Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and radical Islamist movements from imperial divide-and-rule through 7/7, the Arab Spring, and Syria.
How the British Invented Communism (And Blamed It on the Jews) (Poe, 2024) — Polemic arguing British imperial strategy and Round Table networks drove the Russian Revolution and that modern globalism continues that project.
Treasure Islands: Tax Havens and the Men Who Stole the World (Shaxson, 2011) — Investigation of the offshore system with the City of London, Eurodollars, and a British “spider’s web” of dependencies at the centre of post-imperial finance.
The City: London and the Global Power of Finance (Norfield, Verso 2016) — Account of the City as a world financial centre inside an Anglo-American system: hierarchy of powers, profit and leverage, the imperial web of services and markets, and the UK current-account / FX / derivatives machine.
The Clash of Civilizations and the Remaking of World Order (Huntington, 1996) — Post–Cold War thesis that global politics is multipolar and multicivilizational, with Western universalism in conflict especially with Islam and China.

sources/britain-since-1945.content:
Britain Since 1945 (Hollowell, ed., 2003)
A multi-author textbook survey of post-1945 Britain in politics, society, and economy, commissioned for the Making Contemporary Britain series and edited by Jonathan Hollowell, with thematic chapters by specialists including Christopher Coker, Simon James, Alan Sked, Kenneth O. Morgan, Arthur Marwick, and others.
Summary
Britain Since 1945 is a commissioned multi-author volume in Blackwell’s Making Contemporary Britain series (General Editor Anthony Seldon; Consultant Editor Peter Hennessy). Jonathan Hollowell, of Empire State College / State University of New York and associated with the Institute of Contemporary British History, designed and edited the collection as a comprehensive introduction for students and general readers. The work is organised in three parts—Government and Politics, Society, and Economy—with twenty-three numbered chapters, each by a named specialist, and a general index (beginning at p. 461 in the extract). Coverage runs from 1945 into the early Blair years (chronologies in several chapters reach 1999–2002).
Part I surveys foreign and defence policy, the constitution and Parliament, the parties, the shift from Commonwealth to European integration, Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland, political thought, the civil service, local government, and the media. Part II treats social trends and class, women and social change, cultural change, education, race relations, health care, science and information technology, and pressure groups. Part III covers economic policy, employment and the labour market, industrial relations, and the welfare state. Chapter summaries below are drawn from body openers and structure in the extract, not the table of contents alone.
Source
Hollowell, Jonathan, ed. Britain Since 1945. Making Contemporary Britain. Oxford: Blackwell Publishers Ltd, 2003. ISBN-13 9780470700877 (local file). Series general editor Anthony Seldon; consultant editor Peter Hennessy. Contributors are named on each chapter.
Full raw text extracted from the local PDF via pdftotext -layout available at raw.txt (1,518,903 bytes; 22,670 lines).
Note: PDF extract has form-feeds, broken hyphenation, and OCR artefacts (e.g. “ParIia ment,” “McCuigan” for McGuigan, “0.” for “O.”). Running headers and chapter chronologies sit between body chapters. Chapter boundaries were recovered from title + author strings in the body.
Chapters
Part I — Government and Politics
Chapter 1 — Foreign and Defence Policy (Christopher Coker)
“Britain emerged from the Second World War one of the Big Three: perhaps not a superpower like the United States and the Soviet Union, but the third wealthiest power in the world.” Coker opens with wartime prestige, exhaustion, and debt (wartime debt framed at about £22 billion, roughly $2,000 per capita), and notes American conviction by war’s end that a post-war order could largely be built without British assistance. Yet for the next twenty-five years Britain retained conscription, large forces (800,000 in 1951), and defence spending near 10 per cent of GNP—still playing a world-power role until the late 1960s redefined it as a medium-sized power. The chapter tracks that trajectory in foreign and defence policy after 1945.
Chapter 2 — The Constitution, Government and Parliament (Simon James)
“The history of post-war British constitutional development is very uneven. From 1945 to the late 1960s there was little change, apart from some tinkering with the House of Lords.” James sketches frenetic 1970s activity whose principal concrete result was EU membership; Thatcher–Major freeze; and Blair’s “blizzard” of reform after 1997. He defines the British constitution, then surveys monarchy, Parliament, and government, ending with EU membership implications and political accountability. Cross-references later chapters on Europe, Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland, the civil service, and local government.
Chapter 3 — The Political Parties (Alan Sked)
“The history of Britain’s political parties since 1945 has been one of consensus.” Sked describes the post-war settlement—mixed economy, welfare state, Keynesianism, corporatism at home; NATO, the special relationship, Commonwealth transition, independent nuclear deterrent, and eventual EEC/EC/EU membership abroad—then its mid-1970s strain and the Thatcher-era free-market consensus. He treats the first-past-the-post two-party system, Liberal revivals, the SDP (1981) and Liberal Democrats, and Scottish and Welsh nationalism, including Conservative wipe-outs in Scotland and Wales in 1997 without ending two-party dominance in England.
Chapter 4 — From Commonwealth to European Integration (Jonathan Hollowell)
“‘Britain has lost an empire and has not yet found a role.’ This caustic observation of the American former Secretary of State Dean Acheson struck a raw nerve when uttered in 1962.” Hollowell frames imperial withdrawal, crisis of confidence, and the delayed turn to the EEC and European integration. At war’s end the Empire and Commonwealth still embraced about one-quarter of the world’s population and land mass; British leaders distinguished themselves from occupied continental Europe. The chapter follows the early post-war period through reassessment of Britain’s place between Commonwealth, special relationship, and Europe.
Chapter 5 — Scotland: Cultural Base and Economic Catalysts (James Mitchell)
“Until the 1960s, the dominant view was that Britain was a coherent, even uniform nation.” Mitchell challenges class-only and modernisation narratives that treated Scottish difference as declining detail. Nationalism from the 1960s made independence thinkable by the 1990s; cultural identity showed continuity while political and economic context changed. Drawing on Rokkan and Urwin’s “cultural base and economic catalyst,” he surveys Scottish institutions, identity, and post-1945 economic change through devolution-era politics (chronology through the 1999 Scottish Parliament election).
Chapter 6 — Wales Since 1945 (Kenneth O. Morgan)
“For the people of Wales, more perhaps than any other part of Britain, the coming of peace in 1945 brought a mood of renewal.” Morgan opens with Labour’s 1945 Welsh landslide (25 of 36 seats; 58.5 per cent of the Welsh vote), the rise of Bevan, James Griffiths, and a generation of Labour industrial and local leaders, and Plaid Cymru’s weak early showing. The chapter tracks Labour dominance, industrial and cultural change, and the later path toward devolution (chronology through 2001).
Chapter 7 — Northern Ireland Since 1945 (Henry Patterson)
“At the end of the Second World War the Northern Ireland state, comprising six of Ireland’s thirty-two counties and containing the vast majority of its Protestant population, had existed for less than a quarter of a century.” Patterson roots the Unionist–Nationalist divide in nineteenth-century resistance to Catholic nationalism and the Government of Ireland Act 1920. The chapter surveys the Stormont era, the outbreak of the Troubles, British direct rule, and successive political initiatives through the later twentieth century.
Chapter 8 — The Currents of Political Thought (Roger Eatwell)
Eatwell distinguishes Isaiah Berlin’s “negative” and “positive” freedom, then focuses on political ideologies shaping the major parties rather than academic philosophy alone. He notes émigré contributors (Berlin, Hayek), the difficulty of a uniquely British thought after 1945, the parochial roots of early post-war social democracy, and the transatlantic character of New Right thought after the 1960s. He warns against simple periodisations while tracing ideology and domestic policy rhetoric across the half-century.
Chapter 9 — The Civil Service (Keith Dowding)
“The civil service is the non-military administration of the central state.” Dowding frames detectors and effectors (Hood), and four governmental resources—nodality, treasure, authority, organisation. He tracks post-1945 expansion of functions, EU and international transfers of authority, Treasury pressure on spending, and continuous efficiency drives. Until the mid-1980s change is mostly “fiddling at the edges”; thereafter radical overhaul reflects ideological and managerial-technological shifts (chronology through Blair and a new Senior Civil Service).
Chapter 10 — Local Government (Nirmala Rao)
“Local government has been perhaps the greatest constitutional casualty of the post-war era in Britain.” Rao contrasts the early “golden age” of expanding municipal roles in planning, housing, education, and personal social services with mid-1970s expenditure control and later legislation that restricted autonomy and pushed authorities to the periphery. The focus is high politics of central–local relations rather than internal municipal detail, through modernisation papers of the early 2000s.
Chapter 11 — The Media (Michael Bromley)
Bromley opens from a 1996 Institute of Contemporary British History conference on a century of the popular press and the Daily Mail centenary, noting the redefinition of “popular” as middle-market press shrank and tabloids rose. By war’s end the working class dominated aggregate media consumption. The first post-war Royal Commission on the Press framed “social requirements which grow steadily more exacting” and a new scale of public instruction—launching a survey of press, broadcasting, and media structure after 1945.
Part II — Society
Chapter 12 — Social Trends, Structures, Values and Behaviour (Arthur Marwick)
Marwick covers population, births, marriages, and deaths; class structure and attitudes; religious belief, collectivism, and “secular anglicanism”; permissiveness and sexual behaviour; consumerism and leisure; and crime. He stresses that social trends are shaped by economic circumstances, global developments, events, and politicians. The first part of the period is marked by war, austerity, and recovery; “the long sixties” (c.1958–c.1974) bring striking changes in values and behaviour. Tables in the extract give UK population change 1921–97 and country breakdowns through 1997.
Chapter 13 — Women and Social Change, 1945–1995 (Jane Lewis)
“The most dramatic social trends in the post-war period are also ones that have had a particularly strong impact on women: the rise in the female labour market participation rate, the rise in the divorce rate, the rise in the extramarital birth rate, and the increase in cohabitation.” Lewis examines paid work and family change, asks whether female sexual and economic autonomy truly increased, and balances real change against continuities in unpaid work and care (chronology notes 121 women MPs in 1997).
Chapter 14 — Cultural Change (Jim McGuigan)
McGuigan opens with Launder and Gilliat’s 1943 film Millions Like Us—factory canteen, ENSA, and the “people’s war”—then widens to wartime civilian fortitude, Dunkirk and Battle of Britain mythologies, and post-war cultural succession. A chapter chronology runs from wartime cinema and Arts Council charter through Windrush, Festival of Britain, Coronation TV, ITV, Angry Young Men, Hoggart’s Uses of Literacy, CND, the Wilson years and “Swinging Sixties,” punk, and on to the Millennium Experience (2000). Argument links high culture, popular culture, youth styles, and political culture.
Chapter 15 — Education Since 1945 (Anthony Heath)
Heath summarises three transformations: from selective “sponsored” mobility to comprehensive “contest” mobility (Turner); dramatic lengthening of school careers and exam-taking, then expansion from elite to mass higher education; and reduction of class and especially gender stratification. The 1944 Education Act—free secondary education, transfer at 11, abolition of fees in the maintained sector—is the starting point, followed by the tripartite grammar/technical/secondary modern system and later comprehensive and higher-education reforms through the 1990s (binary system end, Assisted Places abolition).
Chapter 16 — Race Relations (Shamit Saggar)
Saggar contrasts U.S.-style racial fault lines with Britain’s post-1945 experience of non-white colonial immigration and settlement. The chapter maps the rise and fall of immigration as a mass political issue, the shift from economic frameworks to “absorptive capacity” social-cultural ones in the late 1950s–early 1960s, and how party politics managed controversy without a fundamental racial cleavage on the American model.
Chapter 17 — Health and Health Care (Ray Fitzpatrick, Rebecca Surender and Tarani Chandola)
“Health care is one area in which Britain since 1945 has experienced a quite distinctive arrangement compared with other Western industrialised societies.” The 1948 NHS—single service funded from general taxation, comprehensive and universal aspirations—is set against European social-insurance systems and U.S. limited public coverage. The authors treat pre-NHS provision (1911 National Insurance), the Bevan compromise with the medical profession, tripartite fragmentation (hospitals, GPs, local authority services), the “politics of technocratic change” to the mid-1970s (Guillebaud Committee, Hospital Plan), and later reforms through Working for Patients and The New NHS.
Chapter 18 — Science and Information Technology (Jon Agar)
Agar brackets the period with the Manhattan Project (British and refugee physicists’ role) and the 1990s Human Genome Project at the Sanger Centre (MRC and Wellcome). Themes include scale and cost of research, computing, international organisation, warfare and Cold War shaping, public/private funding shifts, movement from physical toward life sciences, and crisis of public trust—framing a history of British science and IT after 1945 (chronology through Dolly the sheep and genome publications).
Chapter 19 — Pressure Groups (Wyn Grant)
Grant divides post-war pressure-group history into four ideal-typical phases: 1945–60 limited sectional groups and Establishment links; 1960–79 tripartism of government, CBI, and TUC, with rising Parliament and media roles and new environmental groups; 1980s decline of tripartism, multi-arena lobbying (Parliament, media, courts), and European-level activity after the single market; 1990s partial revival of more traditional relations (e.g. Heseltine and trade associations). Continuity of routine consultation is stressed alongside these shifts.
Part III — Economy
Chapter 20 — Economic Policy (Stephen Broadberry)
“Economic policy in Britain has changed remarkably in the period since the end of the Second World War.” Broadberry contrasts Attlee-era full employment, Keynesian demand management, nationalisation, and planning with New Labour’s 1997 inflation priority, rejection of nationalisation, and refusal of interventionist industrial policy. He reviews planning and Keynesian ideas after the war, fiscal instruments, then a decade-by-decade narrative of macroeconomic and microeconomic policy scaling-down common to Western countries but told through British detail (chronology through Bank of England independence and EMU launch without UK membership).
Chapter 21 — Employment and the Labour Market (Duncan Gallie)
Gallie describes radical restructuring: service employment majority from the later 1960s (52 per cent in 1971 to 67 per cent by 1991), manufacturing employment collapse, technological change from the 1980s, rising workforce skills, increased women’s participation, and late-century decline in employee security via weaker unions, short-term contracts, and high unemployment. Regional specialisation made the transition uneven. Policy markers include the New Deal, National Minimum Wage, and Employment Relations Act (1998–99).
Chapter 22 — Industrial and Labour Relations (Chris Wrigley)
“British industrial relations were often a controversial political area in the half-century after the Second World War.” Wrigley challenges simple “British disease” stereotypes while acknowledging poor relations’ contribution to relative economic performance. He traces Conservative hostility to unions (except the decade after 1945, when Churchill called them essential), anti-union popular culture, incomes policies, and late-century legislation including the Trade Union Reform and Employment Rights Act (1993), National Minimum Wage Act (1998), and Employment Relations Act (1999).
Chapter 23 — The Welfare State Since 1945 (Helen Fawcett)
Fawcett opens with Blair’s 1997 pledge to “modernise” the welfare state and the 1999 Beveridge Memorial Lecture’s critique of post-war arrangements as ineffective for the modern age. She focuses on income maintenance—anti-poverty protection for those unable to work and aid for the low-paid—and argues that both Labour and Conservative governments struggled with the late-1940s Beveridge legacy (Social Insurance and Allied Services, Cmd 6404). The framework of 1945–51 legislation remains central even as structures evolve over fifty years.
Sources

Hollowell, Jonathan, ed. Britain Since 1945. Making Contemporary Britain. Oxford: Blackwell Publishers Ltd, 2003. ISBN-13 9780470700877.

sources/century-of-war.title: A Century of War
sources/century-of-war.content:
A Century of War: Anglo-American Oil Politics and the New World Order (Engdahl)
A long geopolitical history arguing that control of world petroleum has been the decisive stake of Anglo-American grand strategy from the late nineteenth-century British Empire through two world wars, the interwar oil settlements, Bretton Woods, the 1970s oil shocks, and early twenty-first-century wars in the Middle East and Central Asia.
Summary
F. William Engdahl’s A Century of War presents twentieth- and early twenty-first-century international politics as a continuous struggle to secure and control world oil reserves. The narrative begins with Britain’s late-Victorian crisis of free-trade empire—sterling, sea power, and raw-materials monopoly as the three “pillars”—and follows British, then Anglo-American, oil and financial policy through the First World War, the Middle Eastern settlement, the Federal Reserve and New York’s challenge to the City of London, interwar German and Soviet oil contests, the rise of Hitler as (in Engdahl’s account) a British geopolitical instrument, postwar decolonisation and Mossadegh, Gaullist Europe, Eurodollars, the 1973 oil shock and petrodollar order, IMF debt crises, and post–Cold War energy geopolitics culminating in the “war on terror” and contest with Russian energy power.
The local extract is a revised English edition published by edition.engdahl (Wiesbaden), with a 2004 preface framing the Iraq war as oil geopolitics and a 2011 apparatus including appendices on the Trilateral Commission’s 1973 founding members and a May 1973 Bilderberg meeting at Saltsjöbaden. The book is organized in thirteen chapters plus two appendices. Chapter titles and section headings below follow the table of contents and body openers in the extract; the work is a continuous argumentative history rather than an archival monograph, and summaries are drawn from body text, not the TOC alone.
Source
Engdahl, F. William. A Century of War: Anglo-American Oil Politics and the New World Order. Revised English edition. Wiesbaden: edition.engdahl, 2011. First English edition 1992. Local file ISBN 978-3-9813263-2-1. Copyright and imprint details follow the local Anna’s Archive epub extract.
Full raw text extracted from the local epub available at raw.txt (707,142 bytes).
Note: The extract includes a 2004 preface on the Iraq war and oil, chapter endnotes, and two appendices listing Trilateral Commission founders (1973) and selected Bilderberg participants at Saltsjöbaden (May 11–13, 1973). OCR/layout is generally clean relative to scan-derived books in this series.
Chapters
Preface (2004)
Engdahl frames the post-9/11 wars and the 2003 Iraq invasion as the latest phase of a century-long contest over oil. He presents the book as an account of how Anglo-American policy elites used oil control, finance, and geopolitics—drawing on Halford Mackinder’s world-island logic—to shape the international order, and he positions the revised edition as an update that carries that thesis into the early twenty-first century.
Chapter 1 — The Three Pillars of the British Empire
“No other element has shaped the history of the past one hundred years so much as the fight to secure and control the world’s reserves of petroleum.” Britain at the end of the 1890s is described as pre-eminent in politics, arms, and economy, yet rotting internally. Engdahl names three pillars of British power after Waterloo: naval and shipping supremacy; City of London credit and bills of exchange under the Bank of England and sterling; and geopolitical domination of major raw materials. Free trade after the Corn Law repeal (1846), The Economist, and a cheap-labour imperial system are presented as the economic strategy that enriched merchant banks (including opium-trade profits) while undermining domestic industry and agriculture. “Informal empire,” client states, balance of power, and the fusion of City commercial power with secret intelligence complete the late-Victorian picture that, in Engdahl’s account, sets up the turn to oil.
Chapter 2 — The Great Depression of 1873 and the End of Easy Leadership
The free-trade transformation and Bank of England interest-rate policy after the 1857 panic are blamed for industrial underinvestment and the Great Depression that hit Britain from the early 1870s. Foreign lending collapses; British manufactures lose ground at international exhibitions; by the 1890s easy industrial leadership is over. Malthusian free-trade dogma is declared doomed, and the elite debate over how to maintain empire opens the door to geopolitical remedies—setting the stage for the oil century.
Chapter 3 — A Global Fight for Control of Petroleum Begins
Germany’s industrial, shipping, and naval rise after unification is contrasted with Britain’s retardation. German merchant tonnage, Hamburg–American and North German Lloyd concentration, Tirpitz’s navy laws, and the Dreadnought race make Germany, in British eyes, the principal threat. Sir Llewellyn Woodward is quoted on Germany’s right to a navy commensurate with its trade. By about 1910, Engdahl argues, dramatic remedies—including war—were under discussion in London as answers to German economic emergence.
Chapter 4 — Oil Becomes the Weapon, the Great War
The chapter develops pre-1914 British strategy against Germany: fear of Continental economic strength, the Fashoda crisis, the disruption of Hanotaux’s Franco-German normalisation, the Dreyfus Affair’s political use, and the Entente Cordiale under Delcassé. Oil enters as the strategic resource of modern fleets and armies. British policy is presented as steering Europe toward a war that would break German industrial power and secure Middle Eastern oil for Britain and its allies.
Chapter 5 — Combined and Uneven: Versailles and the Redrawing of the Map
Post-1918 Middle Eastern diplomacy: Sykes–Picot, contradictory promises to the Arabs (Husain, Lawrence), “selling the same horse twice,” zones of temporary military occupation, and Lloyd George’s private claim on Mosul oil. Arthur Balfour’s letter to Lord Rothschild is treated as part of the same settlement logic. Britain’s roughly one-million-strong wartime Middle Eastern military presence underwrites the carve-up that places key oil zones under British or British-aligned control despite wartime pledges.
Chapter 6 — The Anglo-Americans Close Ranks
U.S. entry into the war, the Federal Reserve Act (1913), Liberty Loans, and the rise of Morgan and New York finance are presented as shifting the centre of world credit. Thomas Lamont, Bernard Baruch, and John Foster Dulles at Versailles; war-debt politics; and the founding of coordinated Anglo-American institutes—Lionel Curtis, the Royal Institute of International Affairs, and the New York Council on Foreign Relations—frame the 1920s as a decade of bitter yet interlocking struggle over debts, rubber, naval parity, and sterling–dollar relations, ending in a working Anglo-American condominium over oil and finance.
Chapter 7 — Oil and the New World Order of the 1920s
Rapallo (1922) shocks Genoa: German–Soviet economic rapprochement threatens British hopes of exclusive access to Russian oil. Shell’s Deterding, Churchill’s support for White counter-revolution, the Lockhart–Reilly intrigues, and the later shift to trade opening are set against American bids via Harry Sinclair and Standard interests. The chapter maps interwar contests for Caucasian and Middle Eastern oil within the new Anglo-American order.
Chapter 8 — Banking, Depression, and the ‘Hitler Project’
The 1931 financial crisis, Creditanstalt, Montagu Norman, and the credit squeeze on Germany lead into Engdahl’s account of Hjalmar Schacht’s resignation from the Reichsbank and alleged organisation of finance for Hitler. British policy is said to have fostered a “Hitler Project” as a geopolitical instrument against the Soviet Union and the European balance; American consular and military reporting on early National Socialism is cited to show elite awareness of the movement’s character.
Chapter 9 — A New Empire and a New World War
Wartime and immediate postwar oil politics, the preservation of British stakes in Persia/Iran, and the transition into the Cold War oil order. The chapter bridges Second World War outcomes to the 1950s crises of formal empire and the defence of Anglo-Iranian oil.
Chapter 10 — Europe, Japan and a Response to the Oil Shock / Postwar Continuities
(Body sequence in the extract moves through Mossadegh and Anglo-Iranian Oil, European recovery and the Common Market, de Gaulle–Adenauer independence, Kennedy-era Anglo-American design against European autonomy, dollar drain, Eurodollars, and sterling’s weakness.) Mossadegh’s challenge to Anglo-Iranian monopoly, BBC propaganda, and refusal of 50–50 terms set up the 1953 overthrow as oil geopolitics. De Gaulle’s return, force de frappe, and Franco-German accords alarm Washington and London. Eurodollar markets and City revival after Kennedy-era capital controls are presented as restoring London’s financial role inside a dollar system under strain—preface to the 1970s oil shock.
Chapter 11 — Imposing the New World Order
Paul Volcker’s interest-rate shock as a “British model”; gunboat diplomacy and Mexico; IMF conditionality as a 1920s replay; Reagan-era consequences; the fall of the Berlin Wall as a panic for some circles; Saddam Hussein, Desert Storm, and the “New World Order”; and the targeting of an independent Europe and Japan. Petrodollar recycling and debt crisis discipline the developing world and reassert Anglo-American financial power after the 1973–74 price explosion (treated in the preceding oil-shock material: Bilderberg 1973, Kissinger and the Yom Kippur war, OPEC’s 70 percent rise).
Chapter 12 — From Evil Empire to the Axis of Evil
After the Soviet collapse, a search for a new bogeyman; the wounding of Japan as lead “flying goose”; the Asian financial crisis as “hunting Asian Tigers”; Washington’s return to Mackinder; Russia under IMF “third world cure”; Yugoslavia and Balkan oil geopolitics. The chapter argues that post–Cold War interventions continue the same energy and financial logic under new ideological labels.
Chapter 13 — A New Millennium for Oil Geopolitics
Bush and the return of big oil to Washington; “where the prize ultimately lies”; the Project for the New American Century; war on terror versus war on oil from Kabul to Baghdad; Putin’s energy card and efforts to control Russian spigots; bases and “full spectrum dominance.” The Iraq and Afghan wars are read as contests over pipelines, reserves, and strategic denial rather than solely counter-terrorism.
Appendix I — Founding Members of the Trilateral Commission (1973)
List of founding members, offered as documentation of the elite network Engdahl associates with 1970s oil and monetary redesign.
Appendix II — Saltsjöbaden Bilderberg Meeting, May 11–13, 1973
Partial list of participants (including oil and banking figures such as Robert O. Anderson and Lord Greenhill of BP), used to support the claim that a small Anglo-American circle planned a major assault on industrial growth via oil-price strategy before the October 1973 war.

sources/clash-of-civilizations.title: The Clash of Civilizations
sources/clash-of-civilizations.content:
The Clash of Civilizations and the Remaking of World Order (Huntington)
Samuel P. Huntington’s major statement of the post–Cold War claim that the primary pattern of global conflict is civilizational: multipolar multicivilizational politics, a shifting balance away from Western dominance, core-state hierarchies within civilizations, fault-line wars, and a West that must renew itself without mistaking its culture for universal destiny.
Summary
Expanded from Huntington’s Summer 1993 Foreign Affairs article “The Clash of Civilizations?,” this 1996 Simon & Schuster book is explicitly “not intended to be a work of social science” but an interpretation of evolving global politics whose test is usefulness, not completeness. The preface records Bradley Lecture origins, Olin and Smith Richardson support, and readers including Michael C. Desch, Robert O. Keohane, Fareed Zakaria, and R. Scott Zimmerman. Five parts structure the argument: (I) a world of civilizations; (II) the shifting balance of civilizations; (III) the emerging civilizational order; (IV) clashes of civilizations; (V) the future of civilizations. Central theme: culture and cultural identities—at the broadest level, civilization identities—shape patterns of cohesion, disintegration, and conflict after the Cold War. Flags, crosses, and crescents replace free-world/communist banners. The West’s universalist pretensions bring conflict especially with Islam and with rising Asian civilizations; survival of the West requires Americans to reaffirm Western identity and Westerners to abandon universalism and unite to renew their civilization.
Source
Huntington, Samuel P. The Clash of Civilizations and the Remaking of World Order. New York: Simon & Schuster, 1996. Dedication to Nancy, “who has endured ‘the clash’ with a smile.” Local Anna’s Archive epub extract.

Chapters
Preface
The 1993 article drew exceptional interest, misrepresentation, and controversy; the book explores the hypothesis at length. It is an interpretation of global political evolution, not a complete social-scientific theory. Acknowledgments of foundation support and manuscript readers; signed S.P.H.
Part I — A World of Civilizations
Chapter 1 — The New Era in World Politics
Opens with a January 3, 1992 Russian–American scholars’ meeting and post–Cold War identity shifts: Sarajevo crowds waving Saudi and Turkish flags (April 1994); Los Angeles marchers under Mexican flags against Proposition 187 (October 1994). “In the post-Cold War world flags count and so do other symbols of cultural identity.” Five-part roadmap: multipolar multicivilizational politics; shifting balance (West relative decline, Asian rise, Islam demographic surge); civilization-based order (kin-country clustering, core states); Western universalism in conflict with other civilizations (especially Islam and China); Western renewal without universalist illusion, to avoid global civilizational war. Subsection “A Multipolar, Multicivilizational World” contrasts 1920 West-and-Rest, 1960s Cold War map, and post-1990 map of civilizations.
Chapter 2 — Civilizations in History and Today
What civilizations are: the highest cultural grouping short of humanity; historical roster and contemporary major civilizations (Western, Latin American, Islamic, Sinic, Hindu, Orthodox, Japanese, African, and related debates); why civilizations will shape the next pattern of conflict.
Chapter 3 — A Universal Civilization? Modernization and Westernization
Rejects the idea that modernization equals Westernization or produces a single universal civilization. Alternative responses to the West; language and religion data; distinction between modernisation and cultural Westernisation.
Part II — The Shifting Balance of Civilizations
Chapter 4 — The Fading of the West: Power, Culture, and Indigenization
Western power as dominance in relative decline: territory, population, economic product, military capability. Cultural indigenization as non-Western societies modernise on their own terms.
Chapter 5 — Economics, Demography, and the Challenger Civilizations
Asian economic dynamism and Islamic demographic growth as the two major challenger trends reshaping the civilizational balance.
Part III — The Emerging Order of Civilizations
Chapter 6 — The Cultural Reconfiguration of Global Politics
Politics of identity; culture and economic association; the end of simple Third World/Second World frames; groping for civilizational groupings.
Chapter 7 — Core States, Concentric Circles, and Civilizational Order
Order within civilizations via core states and concentric circles of lesser powers and kin communities; conditions for civilizational order and disorder where core states are absent (e.g. Islam).
Part IV — Clashes of Civilizations
Chapter 8 — The West and the Rest: Intercivilizational Issues
Western universalism, weapons proliferation, human rights and democracy promotion, and immigration as flashpoints between the West and other civilizations.
Chapter 9 — The Global Politics of Civilizations
Alignment patterns, kin-country rallying, and civilizational “international relations” replacing bipolar ideology.
Chapter 10 — From Transition Wars to Fault Line Wars
Early post–Cold War transition conflicts give way to fault-line wars along civilizational borders (Balkans, Caucasus, South Asia, etc.).
Chapter 11 — The Dynamics of Fault Line Wars
How fault-line wars escalate, draw in core states, and resist settlement; rules of thumb for limiting them.
Part V — The Future of Civilizations
Chapter 12 — The West, Civilizations, and Civilization
Can the West renew itself? The West in the world; the danger of civilizational war; the common interest of civilizations in order and in a thin global civilization of rules without Western cultural homogenization. Americans must reaffirm Western identity; Westerners must abandon universalism.

sources/devils-game.content:
Devil’s Game: How the United States Helped Unleash Fundamentalist Islam (Dreyfuss)
An American Empire Project history arguing that U.S. policy, following and intersecting British imperial practice, spent six decades cultivating political Islam and the Islamic right as instruments against communism, nationalism, and regional rivals—and thereby helped create the conditions for contemporary Islamist terrorism.
Summary
Robert Dreyfuss’s Devil’s Game opens an “unwritten chapter” of Cold War and post–Cold War history: American cultivation, manipulation, and double-crossing of Islamist forces from the late nineteenth-century British experiment with pan-Islam through Roosevelt’s Saudi encounter, the Muslim Brotherhood, the wars against Nasser and Mossadegh, Eisenhower’s Islamic “king” strategy, Sadat’s restoration of the Brotherhood, Islamic banking, Israeli patronage of Islamists against the PLO, the Iranian revolution, the Afghan and Central Asian jihads, and the post-1991 debate over a “clash of civilizations.” The thesis is not that the United States created Islam or fundamentalism, but that it systematically preferred the Islamic right to secular nationalists and leftists, and that this preference had lasting strategic costs culminating in 9/11 and the war on terror.
The book is organized in twelve numbered chapters plus introduction, notes, and acknowledgments. Chapter summaries below follow body openers in the local extract. Dreyfuss writes as an investigative journalist and foreign-policy critic within the American Empire Project series; the work synthesizes interviews (including diplomats such as Hermann Eilts), secondary literature, and declassified or published policy history rather than a single archival campaign.
Source
Dreyfuss, Robert. Devil’s Game: How the United States Helped Unleash Fundamentalist Islam. New York: Metropolitan Books / Henry Holt and Company (American Empire Project), 2005. Local Anna’s Archive epub extract.
Full raw text extracted from the local epub available at raw.txt (852,094 bytes).
Chapters
Introduction
Dreyfuss states that there is an unwritten chapter in Cold War and New World Order history: how the United States helped create the Islamist threat it later declared war upon. Over six decades Washington cultivated Islamists, used them against the USSR and against Third World nationalists, and misread the difference between the religion of Islam and political Islam. Stages are sketched: 1950s enemies Nasser and Mossadegh; 1960s spread of Arab socialism; 1970s Islamists as props of U.S. allies; post-1979 failure to learn from Iran; 1990s uncertainty after the Cold War; then 9/11 and neoconservative “clash of civilizations” framing. Early American Middle East ignorance (Twain, missionaries, oil) and FDR’s shipboard meeting with Ibn Saud introduce the long engagement. The introduction closes with policy prescriptions: address grievances, abandon imperial pretensions and force deployments that feed jihad, stop imposing preferences, and end bellicose threats—arguing that a “war on terrorism” alone is the wrong response to political Islam.
Chapter 1 — Imperial Pan-Islam
“In 1885, exactly one hundred years before officials of the Reagan administration made a secret initiative toward Ayatollah Khomeini’s Iran,” a Persian-Afghan activist meets British intelligence and foreign-policy officials in London to propose a controversial idea about mobilising Islam. The chapter roots later American practice in nineteenth-century British experiments with pan-Islam as a tool of empire and Great Game competition—setting the pattern of Western powers treating Islamic solidarity as a geopolitical instrument.
Chapter 2 — England’s Brothers
In the post–World War I struggle to maintain empire, Britain makes deals with “many devils,” including, from the late 1920s until Suez 1956, support for fledgling Islamist movements in Egypt and Palestine. In 1928 Hassan al-Banna founds the Muslim Brotherhood; the chapter treats the Brotherhood and related Palestinian Islamist networks as British-era creations or clients whose later global role grows out of that imperial sponsorship and the crisis of formal empire.
Chapter 3 — Islam Meets the Cold War
American diplomat Hermann Eilts recalls first meeting Hassan al-Banna in Saudi Arabia, where Banna came “for money” via pious Saudi intermediaries such as Shaikh Mohammed Sorour Sabhan. The chapter traces early U.S. contact with the Brotherhood and Saudi-funded Islamism as Washington inherits British positions and builds its own Cold War architecture in the Middle East.
Chapter 4 — The War against Nasser and Mossadegh
In the early 1950s two nationalist leaders threaten the oil-centred order: Nasser’s Free Officers in Egypt and Mossadegh in Iran. The United States and Britain treat secular nationalism and left-leaning democracy as the primary enemies; Islamist and monarchical forces are preferred instruments. The coups, propaganda, and alliance choices of the period establish the pattern of backing the Islamic right against nationalism.
Chapter 5 — The King of All Islam
After Suez, Eisenhower is portrayed as a poor student of Islam who nonetheless seeks a pan-Islamic counterweight to Nasserism. The chapter examines U.S. efforts to elevate a Saudi-centred “king of all Islam” or Islamic bloc as a Cold War and anti-nationalist project—complicated stupid moves, in Nasser’s quoted phrase, that deepen the American–Islamist entanglement.
Chapter 6 — The Sorcerer’s Apprentice
In the 1970s, guided by Saudi intelligence chief Kamal Adham, Anwar Sadat brings the Muslim Brotherhood back into Egypt. Washington, used to working with Saudi Arabia and eager to pull Egypt into the U.S. Cold War camp, views the restoration of the Islamic right benignly or supportively—the “sorcerer’s apprentice” dynamic in which clients escape control.
Chapter 7 — The Rise of Economic Islam
Petrodollar wealth funds a parallel structure: Islamic banks and investment companies controlled by the Islamic right and Brotherhood networks. These institutions support sympathetic politicians and officers, launder influence across borders, and give political Islam an independent financial base beyond state sponsorship alone.
Chapter 8 — Israel’s Islamists
At the height of late-1970s American security in the Middle East, Israel and other U.S. allies use Islamist groups to weaken and isolate rejectionists (Iraq, Syria, Libya, the PLO). The chapter documents Israeli patronage of Islamists in the occupied territories as a tactic against secular Palestinian nationalism—another instance of short-term instrumentalism with long-term costs.
Chapter 9 — Hell’s Ayatollah
The 1978–79 Iranian revolution catches the United States by surprise and briefly threatens the entire monarchical order from the Gulf to Morocco. CIA and academic panic over contagion; the failure of prior Islamist-friendly assumptions; and the shock that an Islamic revolution could be anti-American rather than a reliable anti-communist asset.
Chapter 10 — Jihad I: The “Arc of Islam”
Iran’s fall collapses one pillar of the Gulf edifice (the other being Saudi Arabia). Planners scramble to rebuild an anti-Soviet “arc of Islam” from the Middle East into South Asia. The chapter treats the early Afghan jihad and related programs as the militarised climax of the long preference for Islamist proxies.
Chapter 11 — Jihad II: Into Central Asia
The American-sponsored Afghan jihad coincides with a transformation of political Islam: from a seemingly pro-Western Cold War asset (1945–1979) toward forces that can turn on their sponsors. The war seeds networks, fighters, and ideologies that expand into Central Asia and the global jihadist milieu of the 1990s.
Chapter 12 — Clash of Civilizations?
After 1991, is Islamist terrorism the “new communism,” and is the war on terror World War IV against Islam? Dreyfuss interrogates the seriousness of the threat, the continuity and rupture in America’s relationship to political Islam, and the neoconservative framing associated with Huntington’s clash thesis—arguing against civilizational war as the right strategic conclusion from the history the book has traced.

Dope, Inc.: Britain’s Opium War Against the United States (1978)
A U.S. Labor Party investigative monograph that presents the world narcotics trade as a single British-centered business and political-warfare operation against the United States, from the nineteenth-century Opium Wars through Hong Kong banking, Canadian Prohibition networks, North American organized crime, and the 1960s drug-rock counterculture.
Summary
Commissioned in September 1978 by U.S. Labor Party National Chairman Lyndon H. LaRouche, Jr., and written by Konstandinos Kalimtgis, David Goldman, and Jeffrey Steinberg under his direction, Dope, Inc. is a long polemic and investigative report rather than a conventional academic history. Its thesis, stated at the outset, is that illegal drug traffic into the United States is a calculated form of political warfare by the British monarchy and London-centered finance, comparable to—and continuous with—the Opium Wars against China. The authors claim a combined research effort of about one hundred people in the U.S., Mexican, and European Labor Parties, with assistance from unnamed law-enforcement sources, and they frame the book as an extension of LaRouche’s October 1978 statement “A National Strategy to Control Crime.”
The work is organized in five parts. Part I retells British opium policy from the East India Company through Palmerston’s networks and American Prohibition. Part II maps what the authors call the production and wholesale finance of “Dope, Incorporated”—Golden Triangle opium, Hong Kong and the Hongkong and Shanghai Bank, gold and diamonds, a “Peking connection,” the Royal Institute of International Affairs, Canada as “North America’s Hong Kong,” and interlocking British oligarchic families. Part III treats North American distribution and “organized crime”: the Bronfmans, the Kennedys, Permindex and Resorts International/Intertel, the Jacobs family’s Emprise/Sportsystems, and a Philadelphia amphetamine case study. Part IV attributes the 1960s counterculture and LSD cult to British psychological warfare (Huxley, Tavistock, RIIA). Part V attacks the U.S. “drug lobby” for marijuana and heroin decriminalization. An epilogue records the authors’ 1978 presentations to Federal Reserve and New York banking officials against the HongShang–Marine Midland acquisition, and a Paris meeting attacked by Betar militants. The local digital copy is a scan-derived Anna’s Archive epub with heavy OCR noise; chapter structure below follows the printed table of contents and body section titles as they appear in the extract.
Source
Kalimtgis, Konstandinos; Goldman, David; and Steinberg, Jeffrey. Dope, Inc.: Britain’s Opium War Against the United States. New York: The New Benjamin Franklin House Publishing Company, Inc., 304 West 58th Street, 5th floor, New York, New York 10019, 1978. Copyright 1978 by the three authors. First printing December 1978; second printing February 1979. Editor-in-chief N. Spannaus; editor L. Frommer. Library of Congress subject headings in the local file include narcotics control (Great Britain and general), drug abuse and narcotics habit in the United States. Includes index and illustrations.
Full raw text extracted from the local Anna’s Archive epub available at raw.txt (701,659 bytes).
Note: The local digital file is a scan-to-epub conversion (metadata title “Dope, Inc. Britain Opium War against the US”; creator field corrupted to “Some Unknown Investigators”; LC name form in the epub copyright block “Kalimiflis”). Bibliographic citation above follows the title page / copyright apparatus and the standard 1978 New Benjamin Franklin House publication. Later printings and editions of the work are sometimes subtitled or marketed as “The Book that Drove Henry Kissinger Crazy.” OCR artifacts (broken words, mixed page headers, figure captions interleaved with text) are frequent; chapter summaries below are drawn from body openers and mid-sections, not the TOC alone. Part IV and Part V are continuous essay sections without the numbered chapter list used in Parts I–III.
Chapters
Dedication (Lyndon H. LaRouche, Jr., New York City, October 18, 1978)
LaRouche dedicates the book to U.S. intelligence and law-enforcement officers who have died or been imprisoned in the “silent war” against British illegal drug traffic into the United States, with thanks to American, French, and Canadian officials who helped cross-check facts. He states that the only proper comparison for today’s traffic is the British monarchy’s nineteenth-century Opium Wars against China, and that the same HongShang and related banking interests, “aided by those leading elements of the Zionist Lobby which have controlled organized crime in the USA and the Caribbean since the early 1920s,” remain involved. He presents the traffic as calculated political warfare and balance-of-payments looting, cites Bertrand Russell and Aldous Huxley on drugs as political subversion, and closes: the fight against illegal drugs and “decriminalization” is “nothing less than a war against Britain.”
Acknowledgments
The authors state that Dope, Inc. was commissioned in September 1978 by LaRouche and produced under his direction as part of an international Labor Party campaign against organized crime and drug traffic, linked in their account to defense of the European Monetary System and LaRouche’s 1975 International Development Bank proposal. The book is credited to a roughly 100-person research team in New York, Mexico City, and Wiesbaden; named research contributors include Marilyn James, Richard Schulman, Alfred Ross, and others, with Linda Frommer as editor. Law-enforcement sources are thanked without names.
Introduction
The book opens: “America is at war.” The battleground is American streets and schools; the “most deadly weapon is dope.” The authors cite retail U.S. drug sales of about 50 billion and a worldwide take of about 200 billion, described as a slush fund for terrorism and the murder of American Presidents. They reject the idea that drug abuse is merely self-inflicted and name the controller of supply, banks, syndicates, and political corruption as “the aristocratic and banking oligarchy of Great Britain”—the same adversary as in the American Revolution and the founders of the world opium trade. DEA-style user statistics for heroin, cocaine, and marijuana are recited (including a claim of over 48 million frequent users of those three drugs). The introduction sets the polemic frame for the five parts that follow.
Part I — History
Introduction (Part I)
The Part I introduction compares America in 1978 to China on the eve of the first Opium War: foreign smuggling, mass addiction, brazen organized crime, assassinations, and shattered law enforcement. It quotes a dope-trafficker writing that a drug-addicted nation cannot become a military threat. A parallel is drawn between the assassinations of Lincoln and Kennedy as narcotics-mob and foreign-conspiracy cases. Nineteenth-century British finance and firms—Matheson, Keswick, Swire, Dent, Baring, Rothschild; Jardine Matheson; Hongkong and Shanghai Bank; Chartered Bank; P&O—and intelligence fronts (Order of Zion, Mazzini’s Mafia, Chinese Triads) are named as the historical backbone of the traffic.
Chapter 1 — Britain’s First Opium Wars
“From 1715, when the British East India Company opened up its first Far East office in the Chinese port city of Canton, it has been official British Crown policy to foster mass-scale drug addiction against targeted foreign populations…” The chapter traces East India Company opium from Bengal into China as a response to silver drain for tea and silk under King George III; links Adam Smith’s Wealth of Nations and Shelburne/Baring secret-committee machinery to both the American Revolution and the China trade; and presents the Opium Wars as enforced addiction for political control and looting rights. The chapter situates Matheson, Jardine, and related houses as the institutional core of the later “Dope, Inc.” system.
Chapter 2 — Palmerston’s Fifth Column, USA
Opening on “The assassination bureau,” the chapter argues that nineteenth-century narcotics traffic was already organized crime, run by Palmerston behind a screen of respectability and through his role as Patriarch of the Scottish Rite of Freemasonry. Palmerston’s “irregulars” in dope trafficking, assassinations, and Civil War–era fifth-column work are called the linear ancestors of modern organized crime. The model is the ethnic secret society—Chinese Triads, Order of Zion / B’nai B’rith, Young Italy / Mafia, Jesuits, Bakuninist anarchists—on a chain of command to Palmerston. American counterintelligence figures such as Poe and Morse are cited as contemporaries who understood the problem; Lincoln’s assassination is treated as part of the same web.
Chapter 3 — Britain’s “Noble Experiment”
Two “strategically important” events of 1918–1920: founding of the Royal Institute of International Affairs, and Prohibition. RIIA is traced to Cecil Rhodes’s will, the Round Table, Kipling, Milner, and “Milner’s Kindergarten” as a recruitment and planning agency for a “one world empire” that would reincorporate the United States. “On January 6 of the next year, Britain declared its opium war against the United States. Americans knew it as Prohibition.” Illegal alcohol and narcotics are presented as two product lines of one multinational firm, with British distillers, Far East refineries, and Canadian/Caribbean banks as suppliers and financiers. Canada goes wet as the U.S. goes dry; Britain fights League of Nations pressure to maintain Far Eastern opium production as heroin is outlawed in America in 1924.
Part II — How the Drug Empire Works
Introduction (Part II)
“The basis of this investigation.” The authors promise a guided tour from Golden Triangle mountains through Bangkok, Rangoon, and Singapore wholesalers; British trading-company logistics; Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation and other British banks; Pacific ports of entry; Canadian banks and “Zionist financiers”; and finally contact points in organized crime—so as to reconstruct the “Annual Report of Dope, Incorporated” (balance sheet, board, officers, subsidiaries). Illegal drugs are called the world’s biggest business “since the days of opium-pusher Adam Smith.”
Chapter 1 — Banking and the World’s Biggest Business
Hard evidence from DEA and other agencies, the authors say, allows only one conclusion: the drug industry is a single integrated world operation from poppy to street bag, better controlled than De Beers’ diamond CSO. The drug-related illegal economy is pegged at about $200 billion a year net. The problem is “purloined letter” obviousness: the traffic hides in plain sight because the British monarchy “organized most of the Far East to conform to the drug traffic” and because black money moves through the international banking system.
Chapter 2 — From Opium to Dirty Money
Price pyramid of Far Eastern opium/heroin: roughly 100/lb raw gum in the Golden Triangle highlands; about 200/lb at triborder collection; division of a ~700-ton crop into heroin refining versus regional smoking opium. Wholesalers in Bangkok, Rangoon, or Hong Kong are treated as one business structure under old British banks and trading companies plus expatriate Chinese networks. The chapter is the bridge from agricultural production to financial laundering.
Chapter 3 — How the Drug Trade is Financed
Financial control “begins in Hong Kong” with Hong Kong dollar loans to expatriate Chinese operators, plus smuggler-sized gold bars, diamonds, and warehousing dominated by HongShang-related entities. Hongkong and Shanghai Bank is described as semi-official central bank of the Crown Colony, holder of a huge share of local banking, working closely with the colonial government, and the “financial hydra” unifying Asian opium production, transport, and distribution. Opacity of Hong Kong banking statistics is stressed.
Chapter 4 — Britain’s Gold and Dirty Diamond Operations
Gold and diamonds as untraceable media of the Asian drug trade: hundreds of tons of gold through the Orient yearly, mainly via Hong Kong and HongShang subsidiaries. Golden Triangle peasants are paid in goods and gold, not Bahamas accounts; the PRC’s share is said to be paid largely in gold across the Burmese border. Diamonds enter as portable, untraceable settlement. The gold trail is presented as a decisive clue that led investigators toward HongShang management.
Chapter 5 — Hong Kong: The World’s Drug Capital
In Hong Kong, drugs “do not merely dominate the economy: they are the economy.” Official addict estimates of 10 percent of population are raised by the authors toward a “safe, conservative” 20 percent (~1 million), generating multi-billion retail cash flow “at HongShang’s back porch.” Dirty money—retail dope, police bribes, wholesaling, gambling—is treated as the organizing principle of colonial economic life; comparison is made to New York’s addict population and dollar outflows.
Chapter 6 — The Peking Connection
Opens with Chou En-lai to Nasser (June 1965) on helping U.S. troops try opium and fighting the West “with their own weapons.” The chapter surveys pre-Kissinger Western and Soviet insistence on PRC opium production, then argues that Peking’s real money is in wholesaling, retailing, and financing through Hong Kong, not only farm-gate export (an ~$800 million primary-export figure is given as secondary). Since the Sino-Soviet split, Peking is said to have integrated external finance with British Hong Kong drug firms and expatriate Chinese networks as strategic policy.
Chapter 7 — How the Royal Institute of International Affairs Runs Drugs and Dirty Money
Command is traced “to Chatham House, St. James Square, London.” Far East traffic is a “British-Chinese joint venture” with Britain the senior partner, impossible without political approval, offshore credit markets, gold/diamonds, and management of retail crime. HongShang’s London Committee is treated as a special operation of top British banks. The chapter maps interlocking directorships from RIIA and related councils into drug, mining, shipping, Canadian, and “Zionist Lobby” dirty-money structures—the “Board of Directors of Drugs, Incorporated.”
Chapter 8 — Canada: North America’s Hong Kong
“Most heroin entering North America comes through Canada,” per the authors’ law-enforcement sources. Canada is denied nationhood in the American sense and described as run by the monarchy through Governor-General, Privy Council, and Knights of St. John who control business. Role is analogized to Prohibition-era transshipment. Official Secrets Act is blamed for silencing internal resistance; a minority of Canadian officials looking to the U.S. model are praised for fighting criminal activity that enjoys near-official sanction.
Chapter 9 — All in the Family: The Real Syndicate
Why has the picture stayed hidden? Beyond corporate facade, “the entire world drug traffic has been run by a single Family since its inception”—British oligarchic kinship, not only Italian, Jewish, or Chinese crime families. Keswicks of Jardine Matheson, Inchcapes of P&O, Russells, Dukes of Sutherland and Elgin reappear from the first Opium War to modern bank boards (HongShang, Jardine Matheson, Barclays, Anglo-American, N.M. Rothschild, Lazard). Ethnic underworld partners are called fitting allies of that oligarchy. A long “family tree” / dynasty chart apparatus (including Bruce and related lines in the illustration list) supports the claim that political, intelligence, and ideological support as well as growing and distribution sit inside one kinship system.
Part III — Organized Crime
Introduction (Part III)
Having covered production and wholesaling, the authors turn to distribution: Canadian board rooms where Keswicks and Inchcapes meet “Zionist Hofjuden middlemen,” above all the Bronfmans, for the U.S. market. Beneath Seagram respectability they promise to uncover control of the North American underworld; to treat Meyer Lansky, Marcello, and other “Mafia” figures as a British fifth column like China’s Green Gang; to follow money through casinos into legislatures and the “Zionist Lobby” (naming Edward Kennedy, Jacob Javits, Henry Jackson among others); and to track laundering through Basel, Liechtenstein, Tel Aviv, and the Bahamas into terrorism and a privately owned worldwide assassination bureau.
Chapter 1 — The Bronfman Gang
The Bronfmans are introduced via Seagram and public philanthropy, then as “the biggest bootleggers in North America” known a half-century earlier as “the Bronfman gang.” Yechiel (Ekiel) Bronfman’s 1889 arrival under Moses Montefiore Jewish Colonization auspices is tied to Hirsch/Rothschild colonization and Montreal Zionist elite clubs. The family path runs wood, horses, hotels/prostitution, then liquor; the Yiddish meaning “liquorman” is noted. Bootlegging, Canadian distilling, and later “respectable” corporate and Israeli philanthropic roles are presented as continuous with Hofjuden sponsorship and U.S. syndicate wholesale middleman functions.
Chapter 2 — The Kennedys: Organized Crime in the Government
The chapter asks why the Kennedys stay “clean” despite Chappaquiddick, Judith Exner/Giancana stories, and Joe Kennedy’s bootlegging reputation. Answer: from “Papa Joe” they were polished by the British as the respectable front for organized crime; “The Kennedy machine is organized crime in government.” Ted Kennedy’s 1976 Senate contributors are led by Joseph Linsey—linked to Lansky, International Airport Hotel Systems, Resorts International, and Raymond Patriarca—plus liquor and dog-track businesses. The chapter treats the Kennedy political machine as structurally mob-dependent regardless of any individual policy clash with Britain (as attributed to JFK in 1963).
Chapter 3 — Britain’s Assassination Bureau: Permindex
After JFK’s murder, New Orleans DA James Garrison’s trail leads to Montreal-based Permindex under Bronfman attorney Major Louis Mortimer Bloomfield; director Clay Shaw of the International Trade Mart is Garrison’s chief suspect, tied to Oswald and alleged escape channels. James Earl Ray’s Trade Mart visits and Canada–London flight after King’s murder are added. French SDECE is said to have exposed Permindex financing OAS attempts on de Gaulle via Geneva/Basel Zionist charities and Israeli fronts such as Bank Hapoalim. Mysterious deaths of witnesses and a smear campaign against Garrison end the New Orleans probe.
Chapter 4 — Permindex Unveiled: Resorts International / Intertel
After the 1974 collapse of Banque de Crédit Internationale (involving Evelyn de Rothschild and others in the authors’ account), Permindex capability is said not to die but to be upgraded at Paradise Island, Bahamas, as Resorts International and its security arm Intertel—with Meyer Lansky as éminence grise. Lansky’s “Hong Kong West” scheme for Caribbean gambling, narcotics, dirty money, and Murder Inc. is dated from about 1960 (Lucayan Beach Hotel via Louis Chesler, etc.). Resorts/Intertel become the near-shore headquarters of Bloomfield’s “Royal Commission of High Executioners” and dope billions.
Chapter 5 — The Jacobs Family’s Emprise: Sports and Crime
Dying reporter Don Bolles’s last words—“Mafia… Emprise… Adamson”—frame the chapter. Emprise (renamed Sportsystems in 1972), the Jacobs family’s conglomerate of hundreds of companies in racing, concessions, and sports, is called a leading quasi-legitimate laundry for narcotics, prostitution, and gambling, with major U.S., Canadian, and British holdings (including Letheby and Christopher Ltd. in England). Bolles’s Arizona investigation of dog and horse tracks is said never to have properly targeted Emprise despite his dying identification.
Chapter 6 — The Philadelphia Story
Old Philadelphia Quaker families and Britain’s Japhet opium line converge on Paco Pharmaceuticals in the Sun Oil building—packager of roughly two-thirds of U.S. amphetamine tablets for Smith Kline & French, Rohm and Haas, Pennwalt, and owned by Charterhouse Japhet. Paco is named as the main source of amphetamine “leakage” into illicit channels. The chapter inventories DEA/BNDD/FDA actions against Pennwalt and related firms (fines, Mexican subsidiary discrepancies, opium warehouse “leakage,” Sixty Minutes coverage) as a case history from wholesale production “down to the gutter.”
Part IV — Creating the Market: The British Origins of the Counterculture
A continuous essay section (no numbered chapter list in the contents). It opens with Paul Ghalioungui on ancient Egyptian Isis-cult rites using hashish or mescal for trance, then asserts that the 1960s drug-rock counterculture is a literal resurrection of that cult (including the Isis cross as popular symbol). The counterculture is framed as thirty years of British Opium War against the United States—chemical and psychological warfare plus Vietnam. Oligarchies foster superstition, magic, hallucinogens, and “if it feels good, do it” to keep populations incapable of acting in their own interests.
“The high priesthood”: Aldous Huxley is named “case officer,” grandson of T.H. Huxley (Round Table) and lifelong collaborator of Arnold Toynbee (RIIA council, wartime British intelligence research, Churchill briefing). Toynbee’s imperial-decline theory is said to require a trained priesthood of imperial rule; Huxley’s “Children of the Sun” circle (Eliot, Auden, Mosley, D.H. Lawrence, etc.) prepares the ground. LSD introduction is attributed to Huxley as “designated Crown agent,” with RIIA and Tavistock as institutional psychological-warfare arms. Rock music, campus revolt, and mass drug use are treated as market-creation for Dope, Inc., not spontaneous youth culture.
Part V — The Drug Lobby: The Criminals Come Out in the Open
“Britain’s secret army of organized crime is now out in the open demanding the expansion of its dope market.” California decriminalization bills (sponsor Willie Brown, called a Resorts International lobbyist), post-1973 successes decriminalizing marijuana in nine states, and DEA director Peter Bensinger on Maine as a smuggling gateway are cited. Peter Bourne (Carter drug advisor) is attacked for televised cocaine-legalization advocacy. State and federal pushes to reclassify heroin for medical/“experimental” use (Ohio, New Mexico, Florida; historical New York 1919 parallel) are described as the next step after marijuana. Congressional vehicles named include the Javits–Koch marijuana bill and Kennedy-authored S.1437 overhauling federal criminal codes on a British common-law basis. The Most Venerable Order of St. John of Jerusalem is said to run the U.S. drug lobby “out front.”
Epilogue
On 18 October 1978 the authors met Federal Reserve officials (including John E. Ryan and Robert Mannion) and HongShang counsel (including Steuart L. Pittman) to argue against HongShang’s proposed acquisition of 51 percent of Marine Midland; a similar meeting followed with the New York State Banking Authority. Manuscript excerpts had circulated to State, Treasury, DEA, and related agencies; public meetings and broadcasts spread the thesis. The epilogue answers “How will the powerful men who stand behind the narcotics traffic react?” with the 11 November Paris meeting attacked by about twenty hooded Betar militants (one policeman injured)—an assault French authorities, the authors say, linked to Mossad, with Betar’s Jabotinsky–Begin lineage noted.
Index
A substantial end index of names and institutions (Bronfmans, RIIA, HongShang, Permindex, Emprise, Kennedy, Kissinger, banks, places, etc.), confirming the book’s web-of-connections method.
Illustrations
The front matter lists figures keyed to Introduction and Parts I–III (examples in the extract include rates of marijuana use; Britain’s Opium War against China; Golden Triangle opium; HongShang control maps; illegal gold flows; British gold and diamond syndicate; Hong Kong and Peking sharing the drug take; RIIA–drugs and dirty money; Canadian connection; “Dynasty of Robert Bruce” drug family tree; Dope, Inc. assassination bureau). Many image plates in the local epub are present under OEBPS/images/; OCR often interleaves figure captions with body text.
Sources

Kalimtgis, Konstandinos; Goldman, David; and Steinberg, Jeffrey. Dope, Inc.: Britain’s Opium War Against the United States. New York: The New Benjamin Franklin House Publishing Company, 1978 (1st printing December 1978; 2nd printing February 1979).

sources/how-british-invented-communism.content:
How the British Invented Communism (And Blamed It on the Jews) (Poe)
A 2024 historical polemic in seven parts and thirty-seven short chapters arguing that Britain’s centuries-long rivalry with Russia, secret-service technique, and Round Table imperial networks—not the conventional German-sealed-train or Judeo-Masonic stories—explain the Bolshevik Revolution, the career of Marx, and the lineage from communism to contemporary globalism.
Summary
Richard Poe’s How the British Invented Communism (And Blamed It on the Jews) (first printing May 14, 2024; ISBN paperback 979-8-9907510-0-2, ebook 979-8-9907510-1-9; foreword by Noor Bin Ladin) opens from Churchill’s February 8, 1920 Illustrated Sunday Herald article blaming a “worldwide conspiracy” of Jews for Bolshevism—presented as official British line and press campaign including the Protocols—and asks why, if so, British policy also aided revolutionary forces. The book’s answer is a continuous British strategy: blood feud with Russia (Great Game, Gallipoli, “dominion of the world”); invention of “colour revolution” technique from the French Revolution through communism; Marx as British-connected agent with aristocratic handler David Urquhart; Lord Milner’s role in 1917; a cover-up that blamed Germans and Jews; and a “Third British Empire” from the Round Table and Churchill through the Special Relationship, Kissinger, and the World Economic Forum. Noor Bin Ladin’s foreword links the thesis to post-1991 “communism lost” narratives, the Great Reset, and middle-class destruction. The work is explicitly revisionist and polemical; chapter summaries below follow the table of contents and body openers without endorsing the claims.
Source
Poe, Richard. How the British Invented Communism (And Blamed It on the Jews). Copyright © 2024 by Richard Poe. First Edition, Second Printing, Second State; first printing May 14, 2024. ISBN 979-8-9907510-0-2 (paperback); 979-8-9907510-1-9 (ebook). Cover image: Ernst Sandau, 1913, Tsar Nicholas II and King George V, Berlin. Foreword by Noor Bin Ladin. Chapters
Foreword (Noor Bin Ladin)
“Knowledge itself is power” (Bacon); Sun Tzu on knowing the enemy. The 1991 story that communism “lost” is called a lie; WEF “you will own nothing and be happy” is cast as communism’s heir. Poe’s thesis—that the British invented communism and blamed Jews—is praised; Marx’s alliance with David Urquhart is flagged; globalism is a psychological weapon targeting the middle class; aristocracies may persist behind agents including Marx. Churchill’s 1920 Jewish-conspiracy charge is recalled; the question why Britain helped revolutionaries remains layered.
Acknowledgments
Thanks to the author’s wife Marie and to Noor Bin Ladin; other thanks left silent.
Part I — Who Caused the Russian Revolution?
Chapter 1 — Churchill Accuses the Jews
Churchill’s February 8, 1920 article: from Marx to Trotsky a Jewish revolutionary movement of “astounding” proportional weight; full-page Illustrated Sunday Herald piece. As Secretary of War, Churchill is said to speak for the government; the British press runs a coordinated anti-Jewish campaign promoting the Protocols. The chapter sets up the “embarrassing breadcrumb trail” of British involvement the rest of the book pursues.
Chapter 2 — Leon Trotsky, British Agent
Trotsky’s movements, funding, and passage are interpreted as evidence of British intelligence use or protection—first statement of a claim repeated in Part V.
Chapter 3 — Betraying the Russian Royals
Allied and British policy toward Nicholas II and the imperial family as betrayal consistent with a design to destroy Tsarist Russia as a great-power rival.
Part II — Britain’s 300-Year Blood Feud with Russia
Chapters 4–9 — Old Rivals; The Great Game; “Dominion of the World”; The Riddle of Gallipoli; Double-Crossing the Tsar; Britain’s War Prize
Longue durée Anglo-Russian rivalry: eighteenth–nineteenth-century competition, the Great Game in Asia, ambitions of world dominion, Gallipoli as strategic puzzle, alleged double-cross of the Tsar during World War I, and the revolution as Britain’s war prize—elimination of Russia as independent peer.
Part III — How the British Invented Color Revolutions
Chapters 10–12 — Britain’s Secret Weapon; How the British Caused the French Revolution; The Invention of Communism
Secret-service and political-warfare technique as a British speciality; the French Revolution as prototype colour revolution; communism as the systematised form of that weapon for the industrial age.
Part IV — How Marxism Serves the Empire
Chapters 13–17 — Karl Marx, British Agent; Marx’s Aristocratic Handler; War Against the Middle Class; Myth of the Bourgeois Revolution; The Man Who Brought Down the Tsar
Marx in London as integrated into British political warfare; David Urquhart as aristocratic handler; Marxism as weapon against the productive middle class rather than genuine bottom-up revolution; debunking of standard “bourgeois revolution” narratives; identification of the key British-linked figure in the Tsar’s fall.
Part V — The Bloodbath
Chapters 18–21 — Lord Milner’s Coup; Undermining Russian “Democracy”; Leon Trotsky, British Agent; Letting Trotsky Win
1917 as Milner-centred operation; subversion of the Provisional Government; reprise of the Trotsky-as-agent claim; deliberate Allied/British choices that favoured Bolshevik victory over stable liberal alternatives.
Part VI — The Cover-Up
Chapters 22–28 — Blaming the Germans; Why the Germans Helped Lenin; The German Illuminati; Constructing the Judeo-Masonic Conspiracy; Disraeli’s Prophecy; “The Terrible Marx”; The Super-Capitalist Conspiracy
Official and popular stories (German sealed train, Illuminati, Judeo-Masonic plots, Disraeli, anti-Marx and anti-capitalist conspiracy literature) treated as cover narratives that obscure British primary responsibility.
Part VII — The Third British Empire
Chapters 29–37 — The Round Table; The Special Relationship; Winston Churchill, Father of Modern Globalism; Triumph of the King; Lenin in London; The Balance of Power; Kissinger and the Round Table; From Round Table to WEF; Churchill’s Ghost
From Milner’s Round Table to the U.S.–UK special relationship; Churchill as architect of modern globalism; monarchy and City continuity; Lenin’s London sojourns; balance-of-power doctrine; Kissinger as Round Table heir; lineage to the World Economic Forum; Churchill’s ghost over present ideology.
