sources/peoples-peace.title: The People's Peace
sources/peoples-peace.content:
The People’s Peace: Britain Since 1945 (Morgan, 4th ed. 2021)
A single-author narrative political history of Britain from 1945 to 2020, tracing the post-war settlement, consensus and its undoing, Thatcherism, New Labour, and the years from financial crash to Brexit.
Summary
Kenneth O. Morgan’s The People’s Peace is a continuous narrative of British politics, society, and external policy from the end of the Second World War through 2020. First published in 1990, it appeared as an OUP paperback with corrections in 1992; a second edition (1999) carried the story past Major; a third edition was issued as Britain Since 1945 (2001); the fourth and revised edition (2021) adds Part IV on the new millennium through crash and Brexit. Copyright is stated as © Kenneth O. Morgan 1990, 1999, 2001, 2021.
The fourth edition is organised in four parts and sixteen chapters: I. The Era of Advance, 1945–1961 (chs 1–5); II. The Years of Retreat, 1961–1979 (chs 6–11); III. Thatcherism and its Aftermath, 1979–2001 (chs 12–14); IV. The New Millennium, 2001–2020 (chs 15–16). Apparatus includes prefaces to later editions, list of plates, select bibliography (manuscript collections and printed sources), and index. Chapter summaries below follow body openers in the local epub extract.
Source
Morgan, Kenneth O. The People’s Peace: Britain Since 1945. Fourth and revised edition. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2021. ISBN 978-0-19-884107-4; ebook 978-0-19-257782-5; LCCN 2020950280. First published as The People’s Peace 1990; paperback with corrections and additions 1992; second edition 1999; third edition as Britain Since 1945 2001.
Full raw text extracted from the local epub (Python zipfile + spine order) available at raw.txt (1,736,774 bytes; 9,902 lines; 30 spine items).
Note: Local Anna’s Archive epub filename uses special characters (e.g. ǂ, curly apostrophe). Extract preserves chapter XHTML order. Running title “The People’s Peace” appears on segment heads.
Chapters
Part I — The Era of Advance, 1945–1961
Chapter 1 — The Façade of Unity
“‘National unity’, declared Sir William Beveridge in 1943, was the great moral achievement of the Second World War.” Morgan opens by setting post-1945 interpretations—decline and eclipse versus wartime solidarity—against wartime images of common citizenship and social rights from the 1942 Beveridge Report. He contrasts later Thatcherite readings of war as missed free-market opportunities, left critiques that stressed how little class structure changed after 1945, and technocratic diagnoses. Churchill’s limited traditional unity, Bevin’s corporatism, Keynesian and planning ethics, Mass Observation and social policy are weighed against evidence that war also hardened distinctions. The chapter frames the ambivalent legacy that Labour after 1945 claimed as national mandate.
Chapter 2 — Labour’s High Noon, 1945–1947
“‘The Socialist advance continues’, proclaimed the Labour Chancellor of the Exchequer, Hugh Dalton, in May 1946.” Morgan describes an exciting time for the policy elite amid drab shortages and bread rationing for the mass public. Nationalisation proceeds largely through Morrison’s public-board model with limited controversy; the welfare state is widely accepted; the National Health Service is far more contested. Bevan’s NHS negotiations, housing difficulties, limits of educational advance, regional relocation of industry under Cripps, and more uncertain external affairs—including imperial retreat and the loss of India—define the high noon of Attlee’s first years.
Chapter 3 — The Collectivist Retreat, 1948–1951
After the fuel and convertibility crises of 1947, government and nation move into a culture of “consolidation.” Cripps becomes the public giant of austerity, devaluation (1949), and wage restraint; Morrison’s Festival of Britain idea offers cheer in drab years. Full employment, modest leisure and mass sport, healthier school medical statistics, and class-polarised culture (including middle-class grievance) set the social scene. The February 1950 election underlines regional and class gulfs; external dependence on the United States deepens; Britain’s world role remains claimed even as economic autonomy shrinks, carrying the narrative to Labour’s 1951 defeat.
Chapter 4 — The Conservative Compromise, 1951–1956
Churchill’s return is widely expected as a sharp break; Morgan argues the expectation is misplaced. Balance-of-payments crisis, one-nation ministers (Eden, Butler, Macmillan), conciliation of unions, limited denationalisation, and defence of the NHS and social services define continuity. Macmillan’s housing drive and The Economist’s “Butskellism” label capture the consensus mood. Refusal to “set the pound free” prioritises social and Commonwealth stability over market radicalism; by mid-decade affluence, new towns, and cultural revival mark the Conservative compromise before Suez.
Chapter 5 — The Zenith of One-Nation Toryism, 1957–1961
“On 3 January 1957, the Chancellor of the Exchequer, Harold Macmillan, addressed his Cabinet colleagues on the lessons of Suez.” Morgan follows cut-backs in overseas obligations, Kenya and Cyprus as main military engagements, slow progress of the Central African Federation, and West African independence (Ghana 1957, Nigeria 1960, Sierra Leone 1961, Gambia 1963). Middle Eastern limits appear in 1958 crises; unilateral military action increasingly falls to the United States. The Bermuda Conference with Eisenhower confirms dependence within revived Anglo-American defence intimacy and residual mistrust. Macmillan’s approach to the new European Common Market is wary; at home, one-nation Toryism and affluence mark the zenith before Part II’s “retreat.”
Part II — The Years of Retreat, 1961–1979
Chapter 6 — The Stagnant Society, 1961–1964
“In the 1950s, Britain had offered the world, many felt, a spectacle of hedonism and insular complacency.” Discontent arrives largely from books—Michael Shanks’s The Stagnant Society, Penguin “What is Wrong with Britain” volumes, rediscovery of the working class in culture and social criticism, and scare of criminality and cultural dissolution. Macmillan’s government moves toward immigration restriction (1962); Welsh and Scottish grievances and Saunders Lewis’s Welsh-language campaign rise; Northern Ireland’s frozen Protestant ascendancy cannot escape the same pressures. Youth styles, Bishop of Woolwich’s Honest to God, satire, and Private Eye mark a less deferential age.
Chapter 7 — Labour Blown Off Course, 1964–1967
“Despite its narrow majority, Harold Wilson’s Labour government took office in October 1964 amidst a mood of some optimism.” Early glow covers arts (Jennie Lee), Robbins-era universities, and liberal social mood; underneath lies an £800 million balance-of-payments crisis and an unfavourable world reaction (“gone to Canossa”). Brown’s planning impulse yields to traditional Treasury recovery of parity; political structure mixes competence (Jenkins, Healey) with paranoia and survival politics after Gordon Walker’s electoral failures. Wilson remains master of party and Commons while economic and political indirection blow Labour off course.
Chapter 8 — Years of Hard Slog, 1968–1970
“In the aftermath of the devaluation of the pound, the Labour government of Harold Wilson entered upon a grim period of deflation and austerity.” Jenkins’s Treasury dominance imposes Korean War–style restrictions, regulator tax rises, and hire-purchase controls; by-election losses mount. Defence posture winds down east-of-Suez commitments even as residual Gulf presence continues. Domestic turbulence includes race (Powell’s 1968 speeches; nativist organisations), liberal Home Office counter-policies under Jenkins, and rising Scottish and Welsh nationalism (Gwynfor Evans in Parliament; Plaid Cymru growth), carrying the government to 1970 defeat.
Chapter 9 — The Heath Experiment, 1970–1974
“Later commentators have not been kind to the government of Edward Heath between June 1970 and March 1974.” Morgan stresses Heath’s distant, hard-working personality, absence of traditional grandees, and the swing from Selsdon free-market rhetoric to mid-term reverse: Barber’s early decontrol, then corporatism, industry intervention, and incomes policy. Miners’ strike, three-day week, and Industrial Relations Act failure dominate; public culture and the post-war social compact are weakened. The government exits in March 1974 after confrontation with the miners and unworkable industrial relations law.
Chapter 10 — Challenge to Consensus, 1974–1976
“‘Bleak House rather than Great Expectations’ was how a budget earlier in the century had been greeted. The mood was not dissimilar when Harold Wilson returned.” Minority government, price explosion and inflation, July pump-priming, and the October 1974 “short parliament” election frame self-preservation over innovation. Callaghan–Kissinger working relationship; renegotiation of EEC terms and the 1975 Common Market referendum (public funding, pro-market press, “foregone conclusion”) settle Europe only short-term. Celtic devolution after Kilbrandon is treated as another pragmatic half-answer; Scottish pressure (SNP seats) forces Labour to formulate a devolution approach to limit party defection.
Chapter 11 — The Years of Discontent, 1977–1979
“Britain after the IMF crisis had an air of being a nation after the deluge.” Callaghan is cast as a new Baldwin—cautious, adroit, not an institutional radical—presiding over recovery in 1977–78: falling inflation from a 25 per cent peak, improved balance of payments, and a temporary glow of good news. Unsolved legacies remain: Commonwealth decay, Gibraltar, Northern Ireland deadlock under Roy Mason, and Scottish and Welsh devolution bills whose public support softens. Industrial relations and wages policy unravel as the £6 flat-rate deal expires; hostility to union power and the “winter of discontent” frame the road to 1979.
Part III — Thatcherism and its Aftermath, 1979–2001
Chapter 12 — The Foundations of Thatcherism, 1979–1983
“More than any change of government since 1945, Margaret Thatcher’s election victory was taken as marking a decisive shift in the national mood.” Morgan stresses personality and conviction politics over systematic philosophy; early radicalism is slower than rhetoric because she is not yet mistress of her Cabinet. Howe’s June 1979 budget sets monetarist markers; high interest rates and recession force pragmatic adjustment from 1982. Prior’s cautious union law, limited early privatisation, council-house sales, Zimbabwe settlement, and an initially simple foreign-policy stance show foundations rather than full New Right transformation—before the Falklands and 1983 majority deepen the project.
Chapter 13 — High Noon For the New Right—Resurgence or Retreat?, 1983–1990
Second-term radicalism: large-scale privatisation, Lawson’s tax-cutting budgets (standard rate to 27p in 1987), Tebbit-era union legislation, and the 1984–85 miners’ strike as supreme test—ending in union defeat without power cuts. Assaults on local government (abolition of metropolitan authorities), quangos, Arts Council patronage patterns, press constraints, Church tensions, and universities illustrate centralisation paradoxically pursued by an anti-statist government. Westland exposes dictatorial tendencies; personalised Cabinet power and later poll-tax crisis prepare Thatcher’s fall.
Chapter 14 — Fin de Siècle: New Labour in Power, 1990–2001
Thatcher’s fall is a defining public moment; Major’s likeable style does not cure Conservative unpopularity, yet 1992 still returns a Conservative majority and appears to confirm Tory England. “Black Wednesday” (16 September 1992) shatters ERM policy and economic reputation. Europe and Maastricht torment the party; sleaze and policy drift deepen malaise. The chapter carries the narrative through Major’s decline to Blair’s 1997 victory and the first New Labour years through 2001—rebranding, constitutional reform momentum, and the fin-de-siècle resettlement of British politics after eighteen years of Conservative rule.
Part IV — The New Millennium, 2001–2020
Chapter 15 — Millennial Perspectives, 2001–2008
“The British entered the new millennium in sober and unheroic mood.” Finance and credit dominate a once-manufacturing economy; Old Labour tools seem obsolete. Blair’s personal charisma and triangulation structure politics; public heroes are drawn from the past (Churchill) more than the present. Social peace coexists with stubborn poverty (Rowntree) and sharp class division; gay equality advances as church influence wanes; multiculturalism and post-2004 EU migration reshape debate (Parekh report; “chicken tikka masala” as national dish rhetoric). Devolution beds in for Scotland and Wales while England remains the constitutional “black hole.” Science (genetics) and cultural confidence contrast with unheroic politics through Brown’s succession on the eve of crash.
Chapter 16 — From Crash to Brexit, 2008–2020
“Towards the end of the first decade of the twenty-first century, the course of British history alarmingly changed.” Brown faces collapsing receipts, unemployment, and banking crisis after the U.S. sub-prime shock; 2009 is spent clearing wreckage. The May 2010 election produces the first hung parliament since 1929 and a Conservative–Liberal Democrat Coalition. Austerity, welfare caps, and rising inequality follow; Lib Dems are damaged by association. The Scottish independence referendum and SNP sweep in 2015 mark a landmark for the Union. Thereafter politics is “convulsed by intense and bitter argument on Europe”: UKIP’s leverage, Cameron’s referendum pledge, Cabinet splits, and the path through the 2016 Leave vote and its aftermath to 2020 close the book’s narrative.
Sources

Morgan, Kenneth O. The People’s Peace: Britain Since 1945. Fourth and revised edition. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2021. ISBN 978-0-19-884107-4; ebook 978-0-19-257782-5.
Earlier editions: first 1990; paperback corrections 1992; second 1999; third as Britain Since 1945 2001.

sources/secret-affairs.title: Secret Affairs
sources/secret-affairs.content:
Secret Affairs: Britain’s Collusion with Radical Islam (Curtis)
A research monograph, grounded in declassified files and open sources, arguing that postwar British foreign policy has systematically colluded with radical Islamic states and movements—Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, the Muslim Brotherhood milieu, and assorted jihadist networks—to serve imperial residue, Cold War, and financial-order objectives, at lasting cost to British security.
Summary
Mark Curtis’s Secret Affairs (new updated edition 2018; first edition 2010) fills what he calls a missing link in commentary on British terrorism and Middle East policy: Whitehall’s long record of collusion with radical Islam. After 7/7 and later wars in Libya and Syria, public debate stresses home-grown radicalisation or blowback from Iraq and Afghanistan; Curtis adds a deeper pattern of alliance with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan and with extremist movements and, at times, outright jihadist groups. Both Saudi Arabia and Pakistan are described as partly British creations; Islamist forces have been useful as counterweights to nationalism and communism, as covert assets, and as props of a pro-Western financial order (Saudi investment in London). The book rests partly on National Archives research into declassified British files, plus leaks, admissions, and secondary reporting. Twenty-two chapters run from imperial divide-and-rule through partition, Iran and Egypt, the Afghan jihad, al-Qaida, Bosnia, “Londonistan,” 7/7, Iraq and Afghanistan, the Arab Spring, Syria and Islamic State, to UK terror attacks and the “Whitehall connection.”
Source
Curtis, Mark. Secret Affairs: Britain’s Collusion with Radical Islam. New updated edition. London: Serpent’s Tail, an imprint of Profile Books Ltd, 2018. First published in Great Britain 2010; copyright © 2010, 2012, 2018 Mark Curtis. E-ISBN 978 1 78283 433 5. Local Anna’s Archive epub extract.
Full raw text extracted from the local epub available at raw.txt (1,200,018 bytes).
Chapters
Introduction
During Middle East wars and upheavals, one aspect of British policy is little mentioned: collusion with radical Islam. The July 2005 London bombings killed 52 people; the threat persists (Scotland Yard warnings into late 2017). Curtis rejects accounts that stop at home-grown radicalisation or military interventions alone. Britain has been in permanent strategic alliance with some radical Islamic forces for long-term goals, and has worked covertly with jihadist groups. Two linked sets of actors: (1) states—especially Saudi Arabia and Pakistan (Zia ul-Haq’s sponsorship of terrorist groups after the coup)—and (2) extremist movements and organisations. Roots go to imperial divide-and-rule; after 1945, planners faced loss of empire and two superpowers; as forces withdrew from the Middle East in the late 1960s, Saudi and other Islamist forces filled space; the 1980s Afghan war spawned al-Qaida-linked networks; London often gave refuge or asylum while extremists continued overseas activity. Five uses of radical Islamic forces are listed; two geo-strategic objectives—regional influence and Britain’s place in a pro-Western financial order—are emphasised. Curtis denies that jihadism is a pure British “creation,” citing Olivier Roy’s definition of Islamic radicalism, and describes months of National Archives research.
Chapter 1 — Imperial Divide and Rule
Roots of postwar collaboration lie in empire. Britain often fought Muslim powers and jihadist movements and feared pan-Islam, yet also ruled through Muslim elites: Great Game props for decaying Muslim states against Russia; Princely States and communal textbook policies in India to strengthen community differences; explicit preference for communal division as a “strong point” of British political position. Muslim revivalism challenged the Raj even as divide-and-rule instrumentalised Islam.
Chapter 2 — Partition in India and Palestine
End-of-empire partition settlements create lasting communal and geopolitical structures—Pakistan as an Islamic state and the Palestine settlement—within which later British Islamist collusion unfolds.
Chapter 3 — Shock Troops in Iran and Egypt
Early Cold War use of Islamist and clerical networks as “shock troops” against nationalism in Iran and Egypt, continuing imperial techniques under new strategic labels.
Chapter 4 — Islam versus Nationalism
Systematic preference for Islamic political forces over secular nationalist projects across the Middle East, as British power contracts and U.S. primacy rises.
Chapter 5 — The Global Islamic Mission
Saudi and related global missionary (da‘wa) infrastructures as instruments that expand conservative Islam internationally with Western acquiescence or support.
Chapter 6 — ‘Handy Weapons’ in Jordan and Egypt
Islamist groups treated as disposable or deniable assets in Jordanian and Egyptian politics—useful against leftists and nationalists, dangerous when uncontrolled.
Chapter 7 — The Saudi and Iranian Revolutions
Contrasting trajectories: the Saudi system as a long-term British (and then Anglo-American) partner versus the Iranian revolution as the Islamist force that escaped Western management.
Chapter 8 — Training in Terrorism: The Afghan Jihad
British role, alongside the United States and Pakistan, in the 1980s Afghan jihad: training, facilitation, and the seeding of transnational terrorist capacity.
Chapter 9 — The Dictator, the King and the Ayatollah
Triangular Middle East politics among secular dictators, Saudi monarchy, and revolutionary Iran; British choices among them.
Chapter 10 — Nurturing al-Qaida
How networks that became al-Qaida were tolerated, used, or inadequately constrained within the broader jihad infrastructure Britain helped sustain.
Chapter 11 — Pakistan’s Surge into Central Asia
Pakistan’s post-Afghan forward policy into Central Asia and its implications for British and Western security partnerships with Islamabad.
Chapter 12 — A Covert War in Bosnia
British and Western collusion or facilitation involving Islamist fighters in the Bosnian war.
Chapter 13 — Killing Qadafi, Overthrowing Saddam
Libya and Iraq policies as continuations of regime-change strategies that again intersected with Islamist forces and regional sponsors.
Chapter 14 — Intrigues in the Southern Balkans
Further Balkan covert politics involving Islamist networks after Bosnia.
Chapter 15 — 9/11 Connections
British dimensions of the background to the September 11 attacks—relationships, refuges, and intelligence failures or choices.
Chapter 16 — Londonistan: A ‘Green Light’ to Terrorism
London as a permissive environment for extremist organising and propaganda—“Londonistan”—alleged green lights or wilful blindness serving foreign-policy equities.
Chapter 17 — 7/7 and the London–Islamabad Axis
The July 2005 bombings read through the lens of the Britain–Pakistan intelligence and militant nexus rather than solely as isolated home-grown crime.
Chapter 18 — Alliances of Moderation
Official language of “moderate” Muslim partners as cover for continued relationships with problematic regimes and movements.
Chapter 19 — Allied to the Enemy: Iraq and Afghanistan
Post-9/11 wars in which Britain is formally at war with forces its past policies helped empower, while still allied to state sponsors with dual policies.
Chapter 20 — Good and Bad Revolutions: The Arab Spring
Selective British responses to 2011 uprisings—distinguishing “good” and “bad” revolutions according to strategic interest, including Islamist winners.
Chapter 21 — Islamic State, al-Qaida and Covert Action in Syria
Syria’s war: covert action, rebel sponsorship, and the rise of Islamic State and al-Qaida affiliates within a field Britain helped shape.
Chapter 22 — UK Terror Attacks: The Whitehall Connection
Domestic UK terror attacks linked back to the historical pattern of Whitehall collusion, refuge, and dual policy toward radical Islam.

sources/the-city-norfield.content:
The City: London and the Global Power of Finance (Norfield)
A City-insider political economy of British imperialism after 1945, treating finance as the nervous system of capitalism and London as the world’s broker: eurodollars, FX and OTC derivatives, current-account dealing revenues, tax-haven spokes, and an Anglo-American “double planet” that appropriates value from a ranked hierarchy of states.
Summary
Tony Norfield’s The City (Verso, 2016) is not a dealing-room memoir. It uses a 1987 Bank of America eurobond-desk anecdote and nearly twenty years in London banks (American, Japanese, British, Dutch) to ask how the global financial system works and in whose interests. Finance is not a cancer removable from a healthy “productive” capitalism; it is inseparable from production, mergers, and state debt. Britain uses the system to appropriate value while appearing to provide a service. Three themes run through the book: a small group of states holds privileged positions in production, commerce, investment, and finance; finance pervades all economic activity rather than sitting beside a “real economy”; and UK external accounts and investment flows show how the City finances a chronic goods deficit and funds British capital worldwide. Norfield rejects treating the City as Wall Street’s satellite (Gowan, Panitch/Gindin), as a City–Bank–Treasury clique against industry, or as “financialisation” plus the 2007–8 crash. The US is hegemonic but not first in every market; the UK is first in international banking location, FX turnover, and OTC interest-rate derivatives. A five-measure “pecking order” for 2013–14 ranks the US far ahead, the UK second (index 34 versus US 96), then China. Later chapters track leverage and profit, seigniorage and dollar-payments power, the UK current and financial accounts, and China’s challenge via the NDB, AIIB, and offshore renminbi.
Source
Norfield, Tony. The City: London and the Global Power of Finance. London: Verso, 6 Meard Street, London W1F 0EG; New York: Verso, 20 Jay Street, Suite 1010, Brooklyn, NY 11201, 2016. Copyright © Tony Norfield 2016. ISBN-13 978-1-78478-366-2; US EBK 978-1-78478-367-9; UK EBK 978-1-78478-365-5. Verso is the imprint of New Left Books. Dedicated to Alice and Lucy. Research culminated in a 2014 PhD at SOAS (Ben Fine). Acknowledgements include Lucy and Alice, John Smith, Andy Higginbottom, Maria Ivanova, Susil, and Verso editors Rosie Warren and Leo Hollis. Preface dated London, September 2015.

Chapters
Preface
Summer 1987: the head of eurobond trading at Bank of America International in London asks the new analyst “Where is value?” Less than a year after Thatcher’s Big Bang, foreign banks are expanding in the City. Norfield’s career lasts nearly twenty years, three further banks (Japanese, British, Dutch), dealing rooms, and travel to forty countries. Screens improve; the search for value does not. If the dealer finds it, a portion becomes bonus and bank profit. The casino analogy is misleading: the City’s primary role is managing deals for capitalist companies and governments—the financial nerve centre of the global system, first in line when crises hit.
The book is not a City autobiography. The City does not exist only to launch a business elite, though it can do that. It plays particular roles for British capitalism and could not do so unless it also serviced a global system. It generates dealing revenues from worldwide transactions and easy funding for favoured corporations and governments, facilitating finance and centralising economic power.
A second aim is to refuse the counter-position of finance to a favoured “productive” capitalism. Financial operations arise from market production; large “productive” firms merge, take over rivals, and use equity and bond markets. If you dislike finance but accept the capitalist market, the two are inseparable.
Chapter 1 — Britain, Finance and the World Economy
Admiral Lord West (September 2011) rejects “second-tier power” status: fifth or sixth wealthiest nation, large export share of GDP, world shipping run from the UK, largest European investor in South and Southeast Asia and the Pacific Rim, permanent UN Security Council member—“not bloody Denmark or Belgium.” Norfield notes five wars under Labour 1997–2010 and Libya, but focuses on economic foundations West omitted: corporate ownership and financial markets.
2013 outward FDI stock: UK 1,885bn, second to US 6,350bn, larger as a share of the national economy. FT Top 500 (2011): UK second, 34 companies, 2,085bn market value versus US 160 companies, 9,602bn. Of the world’s top 100 non-financial corporations (2013, foreign assets): 23 US, 16 British, 11 French, 10 each Germany and Japan; the three biggest UK-based were Royal Dutch/Shell, BP, Vodafone (2nd, 6th, 7th). Top 50 financial companies by geographical spread (2012): UK second with six institutions to US ten; HSBC in 65 countries, Barclays 46. Canada, France, Germany, Switzerland each had four. UK-based bank assets more than four times GDP; adding equities and debt securities, eight times GDP. Only smaller niches (Switzerland, Luxembourg, Ireland) are larger relative to the domestic economy.
Finance is not confined to banks. Ford Motor Credit and GE Capital illustrate industrial firms’ finance arms; takeovers, equity stakes, and buyout ambitions are typical. States sell securities and central banks set rates. Under imperialism—defined as the stage where a few corporations from a few countries dominate the world market—access to finance both reflects and retains power. Some 200 countries exist; about twenty count; among those a hierarchy. Birth in a rich country is the global analogue of wealthy parents.
The financial system cannot be understood nationally. The dollar is US national money and “world money”; Fed decisions hit the globe, and world flows condition US markets.
Britain’s “invisible empire” after 1979 and especially Big Bang 1986 has lacked a substantial radical review since the 1980s for three reasons: finance is treated as outside power; US dominance (Britain as “lapdog” over Iraq) crowds out British imperial interest; City prominence is treated as policy choice rather than outgrowth of imperial power. Cain and Hopkins’s British Imperialism barely covers post-1970.
International investment income dwarfs many national GDPs: 2013 US receipts 773.4bn, payments 564.9bn, net about $209bn. UK revenues come more from international dealing than from foreign investments. Norfield criticises Peter Gowan (The Global Gamble) for a US-only view and for treating crises as planned; the City is not merely “a servicing centre for the dollar currency zone and a satellite of Wall Street.” Hedge funds bet on 1997 Asia from assessments of deficits and short-term capital, not US government design. Eric Helleiner is stronger on multiple states and industrial lobbying for capital-account opening, but treats policy as intellectual influence and Britain’s liberalisation as a “lagging” hegemonic commitment to nineteenth-century finance. Norfield: late-twentieth-century UK policy was a forward-looking leverage of the City’s existing status.
Panitch and Gindin (The Making of Global Capitalism) overstate consensus and US Treasury/Fed/IMF political power, understate economic appropriation (dollar funding of deficits as subsidy), and recycle the satellite thesis. US dollar LIBOR is not “the internationally traded version of the Fed’s interest rate”: the US has no equivalent unsecured term interbank market—no “NYIBOR.” They treat latest US hegemony as durable (“End of History”). Norfield notes euro origins in 1970s dollar chaos, possible future euro-area defensive measures, UK EU-referendum politics (2016–17), UKIP 13 per cent in 2015, and China: 2014 New Development Bank (Shanghai, China-funded) and AIIB (US failed to keep allies out); China/Hong Kong/Shanghai/Shenzhen already second in equity capitalisation and turnover.
David Harvey’s “accumulation by dispossession” and crisis focus end in a call for a new “New Deal” and “more benevolent imperial trajectory,” sidelining daily financial appropriation. François Chesnais’s stress on concentrated interest- and dividend-bearing money-capital as legally protected claims on surplus is accepted; high borrowing costs for weak countries are only a small part of broader appropriation.
Roadmap: chs. 2–3 historical US–UK evolution and Europe; ch. 4 institutions, credit, securities prices; ch. 5 hierarchy; ch. 6 profit and leverage; ch. 7 privileges by country; ch. 8 UK machine; ch. 9 Islamic finance, China, and a changing environment for Anglo-American domination.
Chapter 2 — The Anglo-American System
1925 gold-standard return at the 1914 sterling parity is used to show that financial policy cannot be read from the national economy alone. Keynes’s Economic Consequences of Mr Churchill treated only domestic overvaluation (~10 per cent versus the dollar) and ignored the government’s US/Empire rationale. Churchill: if Britain did not move, the Empire would go onto a gold standard of the dollar. Budget speech: US and Germany already gold-related; Dominions in “complete unity”; a “uniform standard of value” like ships in a harbour. The experiment lasted until 1931 gold outflows; then protectionist Empire/Dominion links and, from 1940 to the early 1970s, the Sterling Area.
Bretton Woods (July 1944): US industrial and reserve supremacy. Morgenthau wanted the financial centre in New York, not London, and placed IMF and World Bank in Washington. New York did not achieve the domination envisaged: US banks faced Glass-Steagall, interstate limits, Regulation Q (no interest on demand deposits; rate caps until the 1980s), and the 1963 Interest Equalisation Tax on US residents’ purchases of foreign securities. London specialised in short-term credit, foreign bonds, and a developed unsecured term interbank market. Time zone: London covers Asia morning, Europe all day, Americas afternoon; New York misses Tokyo/Singapore days and the European morning. Even in 1957 sterling still financed some 40 per cent of world trade.
The “special relationship” was not mutual support. US pressure ended the Anglo-Japanese alliance in the 1920s; Lend-Lease and asset liquidation bought US funds and bases; Keynes’s bancor was rejected. Suez 1956: US opposition plus sterling selling forced Britain down. Post-1945 Britain still tried to restore Empire (including using Japanese troops in Asia; Indian troops in colonial restoration). Cold War softened US anti-colonialism; Cain and Hopkins: the Empire became a “bulwark against the Communist menace.” Convertibility attempt 1947 failed; 1949 devaluation 4.03 to 2.80; many FX restrictions until 1958.
Sterling Area: colonies deposited trade earnings in London at a fixed rate and could not freely draw dollars even when they earned them; Dominions had more leeway. Marketing boards bought colonial commodities below world prices (Acland 1951: West African palm oil £94/ton versus free market £134–210). Harold Wilson 1953: dollar problems might be solved “200 or 1,000 feet below the soil in the Colonial areas.” Jennie Lee 1956: keep them as bankers. Groundnut scheme abandoned 1951. By the late 1950s Western European recovery made Empire orientation passé. Colonies began running US deficits; Sterling Area current-account deficit with the world rose from average £508m (1958–61) to £754m (1962–65), a little over 2 per cent of UK GDP, while the UK itself had a modest surplus. Empire deficits added to UK financing trouble. EFTA 1960; first EEC application 1961, de Gaulle veto January 1963 after Nassau Polaris deal with Kennedy.
Pre-1914 Britain had current-account surplus averaging 5 per cent of GDP; ~1910 one-third of world securities quoted in London, foreign securities ~60 per cent of London listings. War sales and exchange controls until 1958 destroyed that. Radcliffe Report 1959: City “invisible earnings” need not collapse if settlements moved off sterling.
Euromarkets: eurocurrency deposits/loans from late 1950s; eurobonds from 1963 after Bank of England 1962 allowed foreign-currency securities in London. “Euro” means outside national regulation, usually with non-residents; transfers of dollars still clear through the US payments system. Interest paid gross; no FDIC on eurodollar deposits in US banks. Fed imposed 10 per cent reserve on extra eurodollar borrowings October 1969; market still grew. Deposits estimated from ~1bn (1960) to 57bn (1970) to 1,050bn (1983); ~90 per cent dollars in the 1960s. Bank of England Governor, Chicago 1971: eurodollar market equal to France’s money supply; roll-over credits, FRNs, infant eurodollar commercial paper for corporations whose needs domestic systems could not meet. US FDI ~3bn/year early 1960s, $6bn by decade’s end.
UK net foreign invisible earnings from financial services more than quadrupled 1958–70 to £439m (0.4 to 0.8 per cent of GDP), offsetting the visible deficit and cushioning stop-go. Bank of England welcomed the market; US banks in London from 9 (1963) to 31 (c. 1971); 160 banks from 48 countries by 1971. 1963: American banks and British overseas/Commonwealth banks each ~25 per cent of London market business; accepting houses under 20 per cent. US banks nearly half of foreign-bank liabilities late 1960s. ~30 per cent of euro deposits and 40 per cent of loans in the 1970s longer than three months—hence LIBOR, no NYIBOR.
Eurobonds: bearer, no tax deduction; IET pushed issuance from New York. By 1968, 60 per cent of eurocurrency-bond trading in London ($15m/day). Early 2000s: 70 per cent of international bond trading in London; 2010 UK 13 per cent of international bonds outstanding (US 24 per cent) but 70 per cent of trading.
1975: UK 27 per cent of international banking, twice the US; Japan seventh, under 5 per cent. By 1989 Japan 17 per cent, Japanese banks over 35 per cent of London international banking by 1987. Plaza-era yen rise, BoJ ease, property boom, then crash: Japan’s international banking share below 10 per cent from 2000. London remained the dealing location even for Frankfurt and Amsterdam banks (ABN AMRO kept FX in Amsterdam, securities in London).
Historical logic: euromarkets served industry and commerce’s scale, encouraged by UK authorities, not impeded in substance by the US. Capital controls later relaxed in the 1980s because all kinds of capitalists demanded the right to invest for the best return. Those flows, plus shifting competitive power (US/UK relatively weaker, Germany/Japan stronger), undermined Bretton Woods. Britain shifted from Empire exploitation and sterling to dollar intermediation.
Chapter 3 — Finance and the Major Powers
1970s: end of postwar boom, slump in profitability, unemployment, inflation, fiscal deficits. UK: 500,000 unemployed a disgrace in the 1960s; below a million a “result” by late 1970s. Bretton Woods ends; international financial trading accelerates. UK and US use the financial system to manage relative decline. Britain’s non-European interests and US security/military alliance make it reluctant to become an also-ran in a German-dominated Europe.
15 August 1971: US ends gold convertibility at 35. Dollar remains the measure of value. 1973: nearly 85 per cent of official FX reserves still in dollars. OPEC price rises (dollar oil, prior dollar weakening): OPEC current-account surplus 6bn to 67bn (1973–74), later 74bn (1979). William Simon to SAMA July 1974: sell Treasuries; weapons and protection for Saudi Arabia. By end-1977 Saudi Arabia 20 per cent of foreign-central-bank Treasury notes and bonds. Oil stayed dollar-denominated despite June 1975 OPEC talk of a currency basket. 1974–79: OPEC $84bn into eurocurrency deposits; by 1979 a little over half of eurocurrency deposits in UK-based banks; nearly half of OPEC 1974–79 surplus invested in UK and US (~25 per cent each). Continental Europe built ERM (1979), a Deutsche-mark bloc.
UK joined EEC 1 January 1973 after Heath negotiations; still called it “the Common Market.” 1975 referendum 67–33 for membership. Sterling Area dissolved in the 1970s. 1974 current-account deficit 4 per cent of GDP; 1976 Healey turns back at Heathrow for IMF $3.9bn loan conditioned on £2.5bn spending cuts.
Table 3.1 (UNCTAD): 1980/1990 merchandise export shares—UK to EU 51.8/57.5, US+Canada 11.2/14.4, developing 23.4/16.1; Germany to EU 60.6/62.6, US+Canada 6.8/7.8, developing 16.9/12.5; France to EU 55.7/63.3, US+Canada 4.8/6.8, developing 23.6/17.6. UK and France’s developing-country shares include military exports.
Maastricht 1992: Major opts out of EMU and social/employment legislation; CFSP intergovernmental. ERM entry 1990 at DM2.95 (not agreed with Germany beforehand); exit 1992 after reserve haemorrhage and two rate rises in one day. Thatcher–Mitterrand January 1990: shared fear of German “mission” in Czechoslovakia, Poland, Hungary—“only Romania and Bulgaria for the rest of us.” Labour’s 1997 “five economic tests”: fourth test, ahead of growth/jobs, required EMU to improve the City’s competitive position. Outside EMU the Bank of England could do QE independently: £375bn gilts 2009–12.
1979 abolition of exchange controls (Howe): not primarily ideology. North Sea oil limited sterling-collapse risk; aim was income from overseas assets (1970s overseas investment income under 1 per cent of GNP). Net FDI+portfolio outflows from ~1 per cent of GDP (1978–80) to nearly 4 per cent (1984–86). US had already cut most capital-outflow controls by 1974; Canada and Germany followed. International bank loans rose two-thirds 1977–79 above $1,000bn. France’s 1981 Mitterrand expansion reversed. US IBFs 1981; Japanese Offshore Market 1985. By late 1980s onshore/offshore interbank rate gaps near zero. Plaza 1985; 1987 crash after US–German interest-rate dispute.
Big Bang 1986: easier Stock Exchange membership, end of fixed commissions, end of jobber/broker split—not a defence of a British clique but scale to compete with New York; many traditional firms sold to foreigners. Single European Act 1986: single market including capital and financial services. By 2012 finance and related professional services 5.3 per cent of EU employment and 5.5 per cent of GDP; UK 7 per cent employment (2.1 million) and 7.9 per cent GDP; Luxembourg 17.9 / 23.5.
Table 3.2 (international banking share of assets/liabilities by location): UK 27.0 (1980), 23.7 (1985), 17.8 (1990), 17.6 (1995), 20.1 (2000); US 13.4, 15.3, 9.6, 9.2, 10.0; Japan 5.0, 7.3, 14.9, 12.3, 8.3; Germany 5.5, 3.4, 4.7, 6.9, 9.1; France 10.8, 6.9, 7.1, 7.8, 6.3. FX turnover by location (April): UK 26.0 (1989), 29.3 (1995), 31.8 (2001); US 16.0, 16.3, 16.0. Currency shares (sum 200 per cent): USD 90/83/90; DEM/EUR 27/37/38; JPY 27/24/23; GBP 15/10/13. UK share of location far exceeds sterling’s currency share. Euro dealing still centralised in London, not Frankfurt. Post-crisis euro banking re-nationalised matching of assets and liabilities.
Metaphor: not satellite but “double planet”—mutual gravitational pull, US larger. March 2015 US rebuke of UK joining AIIB. British state authority over City property rules, not government creation of markets, underpinned London’s postwar role. Burn is right that private firms pioneered euromarkets, wrong that a pre-industrial City clique was “restored.” Industry and finance are partners in exploitation.
Chapter 4 — Power and Parasitism
Holcim–Lafarge (2015): €41bn cement merger repriced after Swiss-franc jump—ten Lafarge shares for nine Holcim instead of 1:1. Finance rapidly reshapes corporate power. Commercial capital (Wal-Mart, Tesco) and money-dealing capital (Visa, FX, commercial paper) take cuts from value produced elsewhere; they persist only if more efficient than in-house dealing. Apple/Dell brand and outsource production.
Interest-bearing capital: M–M′, money advanced for surplus and returned with interest—loans, shares, bonds—outside the commodity circuit. Money-capitalists include rich individuals, boards, fund managers, oligarchs, not only banks. Banks: payments (HSBC 1.9bn US fine 2012), deposits/loans, money-market and FX dealing, proprietary risk, longer-term loans and primary securities (interest-bearing), overdrafts (money-dealing). Brokers take fees/spreads. Asset managers (BlackRock 4.6tn, 30 countries, clients in 100) take AUM fees; hedge funds also take profit share. Insurers (Berkshire Hathaway) invest premiums; worker premiums become capital via insurers and pension funds (Aviva; Dutch ABP nearly $400bn). From early 2000s pension funds entered commodity futures.
Banks create money by lending: fictitious deposits, settled net in interbank systems (CHAPS >£250bn/day in 2011). Reckoning with value production is stretched, not broken; weak countries snap sooner. Loans are assets only if repaid. Northern Rock 2007: interbank market closed before retail queues.
Securities are fictitious capital (Marx): equity prices discount expected earnings at market rates, not invested plant. Government debt has no underlying capital asset. Example: 5 perpetual, 5 per cent rates → 100; 2 per cent → 250; 10 per cent → 50. Post-2008 rate cuts lifted equities despite weak output. Owners get votes/boards, creditor rights (states impose policy on default), and liquidity (sale, collateral, payment). Markets enforce discipline: sell shares, bonds, currency. Issuance and share swaps scale monopolies—“a new financial aristocracy” of promoters and speculators. CDOs claimed residential mortgage payments; when payments failed, prices collapsed.
Facebook 2012 IPO: 16bn raised, banks under 200m fees, market cap over 100bn; Zuckerberg 18 per cent economic, 57 per cent votes. 2014 WhatsApp: 22bn, only 4bn cash, rest stock; WhatsApp lost 139m (2013) and $232m (H1 2014).
Hilferding’s Finance Capital (1910) is criticised: banks do not command industry as in his Berlin-six-banks thesis; UK industry self-financed from Empire profits; fictitious capital is industrial ownership; national rather than world-market standpoint. Zaibatsu banks did not necessarily run the group; Rockefeller finance grew from oil, not bank domination. Political implication—control banks, tame capitalism—fails because monopolists cannot control the global market.
Parasitism: Marx did not call commercial/money-dealing capital parasitic because they facilitate the productive circuit; interest-bearing capital’s M–M′ sits outside it. Broader strata in rich countries own securities, not only a financial aristocracy.
Chapter 5 — The World Hierarchy
“Who runs the world?” is the US—but hegemony changes (pre-1914; interwar British political power; Korea stalemate; Vietnam loss) and the system is anarchic rivalry, not orderly management.
Five equally weighted measures (Chart 5.1, 2013–14): nominal GDP 2014; outward FDI stock end-2013; BIS international bank assets+liabilities end-2014; currency share of FX trading 2013 (euro split by member GDP); military spending 2014 (SIPRI).
GDP top ten: US, China (incl. Hong Kong), Japan, Germany, UK, France, Brazil, Italy, India, Russia. China 61 per cent of US GDP with more than four times the population. FDI: US 6.3tn, UK 1.9tn, Germany 1.7tn, France 1.6tn; mainland China only in the China index (HK–mainland intra-flows would distort). International banking top five: UK, US, France, Japan, Germany—the one measure where UK exceeds US (location; UK-owned banks still near US-owned on a nationality basis). FX currencies top five after euro split: US, Japan, UK, Germany, Australia; dollar on 87 per cent of trades, euro 33 per cent; sterling 14 per cent versus yen 26 per cent. Military: US 610bn, China 216bn, Russia 84bn, Saudi Arabia 81bn, France 62bn, UK 60bn; 120 of 143 countries under $10bn. Five of six top spenders are UNSC permanent members.
Index: US 96, UK 34, then China third, well ahead of other BRICS. 118 of 155 countries score under 1.0. US first on four of five measures. G7 longstanding members all in top eleven.
Corporate nationality: BP is “British” by HQ, LSE listing, and Blair–Browne political facilitation in Russia, though UK residents own only 40 per cent of shares. Dual UK–Netherlands cases (Shell, Unilever) are unusual. Murdoch became US citizen (1985) for Fox. End-2013 UK residents still held almost half of LSE-quoted shares. States back “their” firms abroad; firms still need passports, navies, IP enforcement. “East of Suez” withdrawal: state under pressure cuts military reach.
Imperialism ≠ colonialism: economic privileges, monopoly of industry/commerce/finance, backed by powerful states. Domestic antitrust (Sherman Act; UK Competition Commission) versus promotion of the same firms abroad. EU intra-market cartel cases are limited exceptions.
Monopoly snapshots: 2014 mobiles 1.9bn units, 41 per cent Samsung+Apple+Microsoft, two-thirds with eight more firms. 2011 autos: GM, VW, Toyota one-third; thirteen firms three-quarters. Beer 2013: five firms over half (AB InBev, SABMiller, Heineken, Carlsberg, China Resources Snow). Elevators/escalators 2012: four firms ~65 per cent. Glencore pre-Xstrata: more than half tradable zinc and copper, ~one-third seaborne coal, ~9 per cent grain, 3 per cent daily oil. Top-three bank assets 2011: US 40 per cent, UK nearly 80 per cent, Germany nearly 70 per cent. FX 2012: ten banks nearly 80 per cent (four US, three UK, two Swiss, one German). UNCTAD 2013 top 100 non-financial by foreign assets: 75 home in US, UK, France, Germany, Japan, Switzerland.
Vitali–Glattfelder–Battiston (2007, ~43,000 firms, 116 countries): under 0.5 per cent of companies controlled 40 per cent of international corporations by market value (50 per cent ownership threshold). Table 5.1: Barclays 4.1 per cent network control (1st), then Capital Group, FMR, Axa, State Street, JP Morgan, Legal & General, Vanguard, UBS, Merrill… Top 50 homes: 24 US, 8 UK, 5 France, 4 Japan, 2 each CH/DE/NL, one each CA/CN/IT. Barclays later sold BGI to BlackRock (2009). Lehman weekend September 2008: Paulson wanted UK support for Barclays takeover; Darling refused a guarantee; “The British screwed us”; Barclays later bought pieces cheaper.
An imperialist firm is distinguished by backing from a powerful state, not size alone.
Chapter 6 — Profit and Finance
Profit originates in productive surplus; commerce, money-dealing, finance, and tax-financed state spending are deductions or reallocations, including from abroad.
Return on equity and leverage: if profit rate 10 per cent and borrow at 5 per cent, £100 equity + £200 debt → RoE 20 per cent. US manufacturing leverage 2001–10 averaged under 1. Banks create assets far above equity; “normal” leverage ~20×. Hedge funds lever via banks/margin. 1990s–2000s: US net interest margins from ~4.0–4.5 per cent to below 3.5 per cent by 2006 → volume and trading to protect profit → leverage. Chart 6.1: some majors over 100 (US) and over 80 (Europe) before the crash—four or five times “normal.” A 2 per cent asset loss at 50× leverage wipes equity. Chart 6.2: UK major-bank leverage fell in the 1960s, modest rise 1970–2000 around ~20, then historical highs into 2007–8, then back toward average as assets shrank and capital rose.
Low bond yields (4–6 per cent early 2000s vs ~7 per cent pension targets) pushed funds into commodity derivatives, property, forests, hedge funds. “London Whale” (Bruno Iksil, JP Morgan London, 2012): >$6bn credit-derivative loss after doubling up in a small market.
Hilferding’s claim that banking earns the average rate of profit is rejected: no equalisation mechanism between control of money-capital and productive capital; banks create assets; ONS has no “capital employed” profit rate for finance comparable to industry. UK bank licences ration entry (Metro Bank 2010: first new High Street bank in 100 years; 18 months for a deposit licence).
Bank assets largely short-term lending to the rest of finance and secondary securities, not new plant. UK 2011 GFCF £215bn versus under £23bn new UK equity issues. Table 6.1 (UK MFI financial balance sheet) and derivative notional-versus-value discussion support treating derivatives cautiously in national accounts.
US corporate profit rate (Chart 6.3, 1948–2013) and Fed holdings of Treasuries and mortgage securities (Chart 6.4) are used to argue that recorded US domestic profits include worldwide commercial and financial privilege, and that QE props asset prices. A country’s place in the hierarchy changes how profit data should be read.
Chapter 7 — The Imperial Web
Taibbi’s Goldman “vampire squid” is too narrow: the web is the whole financial system, an outgrowth of production and a means for powerful firms and states to extract value.
Dollar invoicing: ~100 per cent of US exports, over 90 per cent of imports; euro two-thirds of extra-euro exports, half of imports; UK and Japan over half of trade in foreign currencies. International commodities priced in dollars shift FX risk onto others.
International seigniorage: NY Fed, Dec 2007, 829bn notes outstanding, ~60 per cent held abroad (~500bn, close to 3 per cent of US GDP). ECB: euro notes outside the euro area €36.4bn mid-2003 to €143bn end-2013 (~1.5 per cent of euro GDP). UK seigniorage after Sterling Area dissolution is treated as negligible versus GDP. IMF 2012: 43 countries dollar-anchored (Ecuador dollarised); 27 non-members use the euro (Kosovo, Montenegro, Bulgaria board; 14 CFA states).
“Exorbitant privilege”: cheap own-currency funding and excess return on net foreign assets. Dollar ~two-thirds of official reserves. US current-account deficit 2000–07 4.7tn (peak 6 per cent of GDP 2006); China’s FX reserves +1.4tn; if ~75 per cent dollars, China funded roughly one-fifth of the US deficit. Chinese reserves 1.5tn end-2007 to 3.9tn end-2014. Foreign purchases estimated to cut US 10-year yields ~80bp. End-2013 US net IIP −5,457bn but 2013 net investment income +209bn—low rates on foreign-held Treasuries. “Dark matter” explanations that invent missing US assets are rejected.
Dollar payments: a China–Venezuela oil payment in dollars clears via US correspondent banks, Fedwire or CHIPS. Avoiding the dollar (CNY–VEF) is illiquid and usually still goes through USD. US can isolate opponents by threatening access to dollar clearing; end-2011 sanctions on non-US banks dealing with Iran; European and Japanese banks paid large fines. Fed swap lines in the crisis supplied dollars to ECB, BoE, and others so European banks would not dump dollar assets or cut US borrowers.
Table 7.1 financial-services export revenues (exclude insurance): 2013 US 83.9bn (25.0 per cent), UK 62.6bn (18.7 per cent), Luxembourg 42.7bn (12.7 per cent); then Singapore, Hong Kong+China, Switzerland, Germany, Ireland, France. Top three ~60 per cent of world. UK financial-services exports 2011 some 2–3 per cent of GDP versus US ~0.5 per cent; sector share of GDP similar (~7.5–8 per cent)—UK more externally oriented. Luxembourg: “paragon of parasitism”; fund-management capital of Europe (>25 per cent of European AUM 2012); financial services including insurance ~three-quarters of GDP as *export* revenues 2011, nearly a quarter of GDP. Switzerland finance 10.3 per cent of GDP 2011; Zug ~27,000 corporations, one per four inhabitants. Hong Kong finance 15 per cent of GDP 2010; colonial opium/maritime origins, then mainland China. China financial-services exports 78m (2000) to 3.2bn (2013); RMB FX 15bn/day (2007) to 120bn (2013), 2 per cent of global. Singapore finance and insurance 11.9 per cent of GDP 2012; Temasek (1974) and GIC (1981), assets probably over 500bn. Ireland IFSC: finance and insurance nearly 11 per cent of GDP 2007; 2011 GNI 19 per cent below GDP—nearly one workday in five owed to foreign investors. Large financial sectors in small hubs are not imperialism.
Equity: takeovers via share swaps. Vodafone–Mannesmann 2000, then the world’s largest hostile bid: ~59 Vodafone shares per Mannesmann share, no cash except advisors; combined value ~£228bn; LSE prominence and Anglo-American shareholders favoured Vodafone. Table 7.2 (2013, $bn): US NYSE+NASDAQ capitalisation 24,035 / turnover 23,285; China Shanghai+Shenzhen+HK 7,050 / 9,665; Japan 4,543 / 6,516; UK LSE 4,429 / 2,315; Euronext BE/FR/NL/PT 3,584 / 1,722; Canada 2,114 / 1,333; Germany 1,936 / 1,383. US four or five times Japan; UK roughly twice Germany. Listing on a major market makes equity usable as world money for control.
Division of labour: US nearest to “full spectrum dominance”; UK often larger for its economy; Switzerland, Luxembourg, and smaller havens take niches.
Chapter 8 — Inside the Machine
London is the largest hub for FX, OTC derivatives, international bank lending/borrowing, and international-bond trading, even though the Fed sets the key rate and NY/Chicago dominate exchange-traded securities. Three roles: (1) international revenues offset the chronic goods deficit; (2) finance any payments gap cheaply and fund British outward investment; (3) give UK-based firms access to world funds. That mechanism is contemporary British imperialism.
Employment: just over two million in finance and related jobs, 7 per cent of UK employment; a little over one million in banking and insurance. 2011–12 financial-services tax £63bn, 12 per cent of the total. Darling: 2000s spending assumed those revenues and stamp duty would continue.
Net figures measure privilege (inflows minus outflows) but understate: without the City, Britain would import financial services. Banking flows are the residual that fills current-account gaps.
Nineteenth-century pattern: goods deficit up to 6 per cent of GDP, current-account surplus from shipping, insurance, investment income. Last UK current-account surplus 1983. Goods deficit again 6 per cent of GDP in 2014. Financial plus insurance services covered more than half the goods deficit 2008–14.
Table 8.1 (average annual per cent of GDP): goods −3.8 (1987–89), −2.1 (1990–99), −4.7 (2000–07), −6.3 (2008–14), −£121.2bn in 2014; financial services +0.7, +1.0, +1.6, +2.2, +£37.9bn; insurance n/a, +0.6, +0.4, +1.0, +£19.8bn; investment income −0.3, −0.2, +1.3, −0.1, −£43.9bn; current account −3.2, −1.2, −2.0, −3.6, −£105.7bn. Trade gap widened more than the current-account gap for ~25 years—policy to expand finance “worked” in that limited sense. 2014 average sterling close to twenty years earlier. 2012–14 investment-income collapse partly BP Deepwater Horizon and US bank fines; also a new net FDI-stock deficit.
UK has the second-largest financial-services surplus after the US; with insurance, the largest (US insurance in deficit). Banks earn more from spreads than fees; securities dealers the reverse. Net financial-services earnings ~£29bn (2006), £36bn (2007), average £38bn (2013–14).
Table 8.2 external bank positions end-2014 (bn claims+liabilities): UK 8,941 (16.7 per cent), US 7,326 (13.7), France 4,527 (8.4), Japan 4,246 (7.9), Germany 4,120 (7.7), Cayman 2,866 (5.3), Hong Kong 2,280, Netherlands 2,159, Switzerland 1,720, Singapore 1,479… world 53,665. UK-owned banks first by nationality Dec 2012 (9tn vs US $8.4tn), third by end-2014 behind US and Japan. UK-linked havens (Cayman, Bahamas, Bermuda, Jersey, Guernsey, Isle of Man) together would rank sixth, 7.4 per cent. Wimbledon cliché (British venue, foreign players) understates UK-owned banks.
Table 8.3 FX daily turnover April: UK 2013 $2,726bn, 40.9 per cent of world (29.3 per cent 1995, 31.8 2001, 34.6 2007); US 18.9 per cent; Singapore 5.7; Japan 5.6. Sterling in only 16 per cent of UK-booked deals. Britain sixth in goods-and-services trade, more than twice US FX volume.
Table 8.4 OTC interest-rate derivatives April 2013 daily: UK $1,347.7bn, 48.9 per cent of world; US 22.8; France 7.3; Germany 3.7. UK+US 70 per cent. Exchange-traded derivatives much smaller; those exchanges mainly Chicago.
2008 financial account: UK banks brought back £147bn deposits and £123bn short-term loans; securities dealers reversed £338bn—about £607bn, 40 per cent of GDP—while foreigners disinvested even more (£459bn fall in UK bank deposits, etc.).
Table 8.5 net financial-account annual averages (£bn): 1987–89 / 1990–99 / 2000–07 / 2008–14 / 2014: FDI −9.5 / −15.9 / −16.8 / +13.7 / +76.8; portfolio +13.0 / −1.7 / +51.1 / +25.7 / +99.9; other +9.0 / +25.2 / −11.1 / +19.9 / −79.2; financial account +9.4 / +8.4 / +22.8 / +48.5 / +104.3. Until ~2004 net FDI outflow funded by portfolio and bank inflows; after 2005 often net FDI inflow.
Net IIP deficit from 1995, over £440bn end-2014 (~25 per cent of GDP). Yet net investment income positive every year 2000–11, average 1.1 per cent of GDP: surplus in higher-yielding FDI, deficit in lower-yielding portfolio and bank borrowing (2014 net bank borrowing 17 per cent of GDP, nearly £300bn). UK outward FDI earned on average 1.6 percentage points more than inward FDI 2000–14, still more in the 1990s—especially Asia, Africa (incl. Middle East), Latin America, mining/oil/gas. From 2012 net investment income negative (−£43.9bn 2014); first modern net inward FDI-stock position. 2014 interest bill on bank borrowing lower than 1990 despite more than 6× the stock—zero rates. Triple-A lost 2013 (Moody’s, Fitch). +10bp on external bank debt ~£4bn/year.
UK financial-services FDI: US 44 per cent of stock end-2013; Netherlands 18, Ireland 12, Luxembourg 6, Crown Dependencies 7; Asia 13 (HK 5, Australia 4, Singapore 2). Only a quarter of total UK FDI is in financial services. UK-linked offshore nodes and dollar recycling via havens appear as part of financing US as well as UK positions (BIS network studies).
Chapter 9 — Eternal Interests, Temporary Allies
Palmerston, 1 March 1848: no eternal allies, no perpetual enemies; eternal interests. After 1945, and especially from the 1980s, Britain became the world’s broker—transaction revenues, not new capital export.
Mark Carney: “we are open for business”; finance a tenth of GDP, one million jobs, large exports; 2050 bank assets could reach 9× GDP if UK share of global banking holds. Martin Wolf called it a “big bet on finance.” Successive UK governments promote finance regardless of stated industrial priorities. EU financial-transaction-tax talk: UK opposed; CJEU rejected UK challenge June 2014; if levied on the location of a party, London could become Germany’s tax collector. LIBOR administration moved to NYSE Euronext; the market and calculation stay in London. Non-dom legal haven; oligarch property, clubs, papers. Post-Crimea 2014 briefing: do not “close London’s financial centre to Russians.” Barclays 2008 capital from Abu Dhabi and Qatar, over £7bn.
Vulnerabilities: rising external debt and current-account deficit since 2012 (investment-income outflows, fines, import rebound). Scottish referendum 2014: 55–45 remain—oil, nuclear base, military personnel, image of territorial security. EU referendum 2016–17: large corporations do not want exit; UKIP ~one-eighth of 2015 votes; mid-Atlantic policy (Common Market yes, euro no).
Islamic finance: interest formally prohibited; structures as shared risk or rent. Cameron, October 2013, World Islamic Economic Forum in London: want London alongside Dubai. £200m sukuk June 2014, first outside the Muslim world, ten times subscribed. ~1.5tn Sharia-compliant assets; 139bn sukuk issued 2012; 22 Islamic banks in the UK (six fully compliant), more than other western countries; $34bn sukuk listed on LSE. Task Force created. Oil-price fall after 2014 a risk to the funding base. Links: Saudi flows and arms, Qatari property, Brunei Gurkhas and Shell.
China/BRICS: 2013 China accounted for more than 80 per cent of the US 400bn current-account deficit but also sent more than 200bn portfolio investment. NDB launched Shanghai 21 July 2015, China ~40 per cent of money, Indian then Brazilian presidency; 100bn capital plus 100bn contingency reserves. May 2014 Russia–China energy deal reported as not settled in dollars. BRICS are not a consistent bloc (US uses India versus China). 2013 GDP: China just over 9tn, India ~2tn, Brazil 2.2tn, Russia 2.1tn, South Africa 0.4tn. China FX reserves over 3.5tn. RMB ~14 per cent of Chinese exports by 2014; swap lines with many central banks; SWIFT share end-2014 ~2 per cent (USD 45, EUR 28, GBP 8), fifth, near Japan. City already ~60 per cent of offshore RMB trading outside China and Hong Kong (US 15, France 10). BoE–PBoC swap June 2013 CNY 200bn—half what was mooted, same as Australia, below ECB’s 350bn. RQFII quota CNY 80bn; dim-sum issuance; Chinese banks eased into London; October 2014 UK CNY 3bn sovereign (first western). March 2015 White House reprimand for UK “constant accommodation” as first G7 AIIB member; Germany, France, Italy followed; Australia and South Korea later. Obama April 2015: “If we don’t write the rules, China will write the rules out in that region.”
Close: financial prices are today’s laws of supply and demand. Do not analyse financialisation nationally or split bad banks from good industry. Marx’s vampire sucking living labour must be extended: relations have taken a financial form across industrial and commercial corporations of the leading powers. The City is a “vampire’s blood bank” taking a sip from values that flow through it; securities are claims on future value—unborn rather than undead. “Only a stake in the heart of the capitalist system, not simply in some of its financial forms, will be enough.”
Notes, select bibliography, and index are apparatus (chapter endnotes to BIS, ONS, UNCTAD, Bank of England, SIPRI, secondary literature including Gowan, Helleiner, Panitch and Gindin, Harvey, Chesnais, Hilferding, Lenin, Burn, Cain and Hopkins).

Treasure Islands: Tax Havens and the Men Who Stole the World (Shaxson)
A financial-investigative history of the offshore system that places Britain—the City of London Corporation, the Eurodollar market, and a “spider’s web” of dependencies and secrecy jurisdictions—at the centre of post-imperial capital flight, tax abuse, and the roots of modern financial crisis.
Summary
Nicholas Shaxson’s Treasure Islands (Bodley Head, 2011) treats dirty money, tax havens, and offshore finance as “the ugliest and most secretive chapter in the history of global economic affairs,” not a celebrity sideshow. The prologue’s Gabon / Elf Affair story shows how formal decolonisation left through the front door and returned through side windows of oil, party finance, and offshore paper trails. Shaxson defines tax havens broadly as secrecy jurisdictions: secrecy plus low or zero tax, ring-fencing, oversized financial sectors relative to local economies, captured local politics, and inverted morality (“taxes are for the little people”). Transfer mispricing (the banana-route example) illustrates artificial cross-border paper trails. Twelve chapters plus prologue and conclusion move from definitions and the Vestey tax fights through Swiss neutrality, Keynes’s struggle against financial capital, the Eurodollar “Bigger Bang,” Britain’s overseas spider’s web, America’s capture by offshore logic, harm to poor countries, crisis “ratchets,” ideological resistance, life offshore, and the City of London Corporation (“Griffin”), ending with a call to “reclaim our culture.”
Source
Shaxson, Nicholas. Treasure Islands: Tax Havens and the Men Who Stole the World. London: The Bodley Head, Random House, 20 Vauxhall Bridge Road, London SW1V 2SA, 2011. Copyright © Nicholas Shaxson 2011. ISBN 9781847921109; Epub ISBN 9781446450147. Local Anna’s Archive epub extract.
Full raw text extracted from the local epub available at raw.txt (776,299 bytes).
Chapters
Prologue — How colonialism left through the front door, and came back in through a side window
A 1997 trip to Libreville for a routine story becomes an entry into the Elf Affair: Omar Bongo’s France–Gabon system of oil, preferential minerals, and political finance; Christine Deviers-Joncour’s imprisonment and memoir; magistrates’ paper trails through tax havens. Gabon is not on standard haven lists yet functions inside the offshore world. Later conversation with New York attorney David Spencer (Harvard Club, 2005) connects African capital flight to U.S. hunger for foreign funds via tax-free secrecy—reframing “capital flight” as destination design, not only origin failure. World leaders’ later denunciations of havens are treated as incomplete relative to the system’s scale.
Chapter 1 — Welcome to Nowhere: An introduction to offshore
More than half of world trade passes, on paper, through tax havens; over half of banking assets and a large share of multinationals’ profits are booked offshore. “Tax haven” is a misnomer: escape from tax, regulation, criminal laws, and disclosure. Spotting features: secrecy; low/zero tax; ring-fencing; financial sector oversized versus domestic economy; captured politics; spokespeople who insist “we are not a tax haven.” Transfer mispricing via Luxembourg financing subsidiaries and interest charges on Honduran bananas exemplifies artificial trails. Efficiency claims for havens are rejected as profoundly inefficient and unjust.
Chapter 2 — Technically Abroad: Taxing the Vestey brothers
The Vestey brothers’ long war with the British tax authorities—“squeezing rice pudding”—as a classic case of empire-era commercial wealth using non-resident and overseas structures to stay “technically abroad” for tax purposes, establishing patterns later industrialised by the haven system.
Chapter 3 — The Profitable Shield of Neutrality: Switzerland
Switzerland as Europe’s ancient secrecy jurisdiction: banking secrecy, neutrality as a business model, and the template for modern offshore practice that other centres imitate or interconnect with.
Chapter 4 — The Opposite of Offshore: John Maynard Keynes and the struggle against financial capital
Keynes and the mid-twentieth-century project of embedding finance, capital controls, and national developmentalism—the political economy that offshore was built to escape. The chapter sets the postwar regulatory order as the foil to the later Eurodollar and haven explosion.
Chapter 5 — Eurodollar: The Bigger Bang
The Eurodollar markets, London banks, and the “great escape” of dollar deposits from U.S. regulation. London’s revival as an international financial centre is read as the hinge between sterling’s decline and a new offshore dollar empire operated from the City.
Chapter 6 — Construction of a Spider’s Web: How Britain built a new overseas empire
Britain’s post-imperial architecture: Crown Dependencies, Overseas Territories, and related nodes as a spider’s web feeding the City—colonialism reconstituted as financial jurisdiction rather than territorial rule.
Chapter 7 — The Fall of America: How America learned to stop worrying and love offshore business
U.S. policy shifts from hostility or ambivalence toward embrace of offshore facilities, tax competition, and secrecy that attract foreign capital—America as both critic and participant in the system.
Chapter 8 — The Deep Drains of Development: How tax havens harm poor countries
Capital flight, transfer mispricing, and elite looting through havens as structural drains on developing countries—connecting African and Global South poverty to destination jurisdictions in London’s web and elsewhere.
Chapter 9 — Ratchet: The roots of crisis
How offshore secrecy, leverage, and regulatory arbitrage ratcheted up systemic risk—roots of financial crisis in the geography of unregulated or lightly regulated capital.
Chapter 10 — Resistance: In combat with the ideological warriors of offshore
Lobbyists, economists, and political defenders of havens; the ideological battle over whether secrecy jurisdictions are legitimate competition or organised hypocrisy.
Chapter 11 — The Life Offshore: The human factor
Social and human texture of offshore centres—expatriate professionals, local capture, and the everyday culture of secrecy jurisdictions.
Chapter 12 — Griffin: The City of London Corporation
The City of London Corporation as a unique political-financial entity (“Griffin”) at the hub of the spider’s web: ancient privileges, lobbying power, and centrality to Britain’s offshore empire.
Conclusion — Reclaim our culture
A closing argument for political and cultural resistance: reclaiming democratic control over finance and rejecting the inverted morality of the offshore world.
